text:
Au-Yeung Yung Mei Charlize 3036567107 
 
 1 From Fast Fashion to Trashion: Reimagining Waste in Hong Kong 
749 words (excluding in -text citations) 
In 2023, Hong Kong sent 402 tons of textiles to landfill every day, of that, 245 tons came from 
homes and 157 tons from commercial and industrial sources (MONITORING of SOLID 
WASTE in HONG KONG Waste Statistics for 2023 Environmental Protection Department , 
2024) . What seems like a small daily purchase inevitably becomes part of the city -sized 
urban waste stream, and specifically, how fashion plays a large role in this pollution. 
Fashion is a social language that express identity, status and belonging, but p eople are often 
blind sighted about the damage that fashion leaves behind because its well -packaged and 
disguised by brands to manipulate the public perception. When in reality, the fashion 
industry is a major -league player in polluting the earth. 
The detrimental effect of fashion is a global phenomenon. UNEP reports that fashion and 
textile sector accounts for 2 -8% of global greenhouse gas emissions, consume 215 trillion 
liters of eater, and contributes 9% of microplastics reaching the oceans (United Nations 
Environment Programme, 2025) . In the context of Hong Kong, the government said about 
17,000 tons of waste textiles were recycled in 2022 , yet the overall textile recycling rate was 
still only nearly 11% (LCQ4: Recovery of Waste Textiles , n.d.) . This has been more than just 
a fashion problem, a combination of city, economic, and systemic problems further this 
intensifying issue (Repair and Reuse (R&R) , 2023b). 
My solution for this dilemma is “trashion,” which focuses on reduce, reuse, and the 
recycling of clothes. The solution I have proposed is to treat discarded clothing as raw 
material for a second life. By collecting, repairing and redesigning unwanted pieces into new 
fashionable items, tr ashion will attract the very same consumers to wear their previously 
discarded clothes again. I believe mainstream attempts at promoting sustainable fashion 
fails due to overtold statements that urge consumers to do better. When in reality these 
firms fail to make fast fashion cheap and convenient enough. A real working solution must 
stay affordable and desirable to the public. 

Au-Yeung Yung Mei Charlize 3036567107 
 
 2 Promoting sustainable fashion does not have to start from zero in Hong Kong. The 
government says there are 187 community used clothes recycling banks across all districts. 
The government also claims that reuse is currently the most cost effective way to handle 
used clothes. Systems such as the GREEN@COMMUNITY stations have already been 
organizing upcycling workshops and swapping events to further the progress of sustainable 
fashion (LCQ4: Recovery of Waste Textiles , n.d.) . Instead of utilizing donation bins as the 
primary resort of discarding unwanted clothes, tra shion would help turn these unwanted 
pieces and giving them a second life. Universities, sh opping centers, and community hubs 
would be places for neighborhood trashion stations where clothes are sorted into different 
streams. A torn shirt could be patched or embroidered, and a dress could easily be restyled 
instead of discarded. Each remade item could carry a small tag or an QR code showing 
where it came from and how much waste was avoided. This feature would make pieces from 
trashion unique as it would reveal the pieces past life. 
This idea may sound too unrealistic, but it brings tremendous progress that otherwise would 
not have happened to unrecycled clothes. Reports show extending the lifespan of clothing 
by just nine months could cut its carbon and waste footprints by up to 20% (WRAP, 2024) . 
However, more needs to be done, as research also argues that Hong Kong needs stronger 
infrastructure, and education to promote sustainable fashion (Repair and Reuse (R&R) , 
2023b) . Trashion can be the answer to all, as it creates new partnersh ips between charities, 
designers, and consumers directly. These partnerships would indirectly teach people to see 
old clothes differently, successfully turning climate action into culture. 
From a fashion industry standpoint, trashion is equipped to be largely successful due to the 
impact on its diverse demographic. First, consumers of fast fashion products get access to 
affordable pieces without being told sustainability is only for people w ho can pay more. 
Second, local designers and workers economically benefit from the remanufacturing of 
these clothes. Third, the entirety of Hong Kong benefits as less clothing enters a waste 
system that already faces serious spatial pressure. Most importan tly, trashion redefines the 
value of fast fashion clothes, it replaces the shame of used clothes by giving the new pieces. 

Au-Yeung Yung Mei Charlize 3036567107 
 
 3 Fast fashion thrives because it hides the real costs, but trashion works because it makes 
that cost wearable and bearable. The fast fashion industry in Hong Kong shouldn’t be known 
for the environmental damages it brings. Instead, the industry should be de fined as an 
industry that uniquely positions itself to give clothes a second chance at life. Before buying 
one new fast fashion item, trashion a piece you already own . No matter how small this action 
seems, it’s powerful enough to change habits over time.

Seaweed absorbs up to 20 times more carbon per hectare than terrestrial forests — should 
governments subsidi se large -scale seaweed farming to fight climate change? 
 
Imagine if a single hectare of seaweed could absorb as much as 20 hectares of tropical rainforest, 
yet most of the world doesn’t even count this marine forest in the climate policy (Parley, 2022) . 
This oversight carries critical consequences as we ’re facing rising ocean temperatures, ocean 
acidification, and loss of marine biodiversity. Making use of seaweed’s immense carbon -
capturing potential through sustainable large -scale seaweed farming can provide us with a 
nature -based solution to mitigate climate ch ange and boost local economies. 
In Hong Kong, water pollution and eutrophication are placing strain on local fishery 
communities. Meanwhile, increasing urban carbon emissions contribute to climate change , 
causing extreme weather events via the greenhouse effect. Globally, climate change drives rising 
ocean water temperatures, acidification, about 50% of world’s coral reef have already been lost 
(NOAA, 2026) , the proportion of category 4 and 5 cyclones have increased (NOAA 
Climate.gov, 2021) , jeopardising livelihoods and food systems. So, what makes seaweed a viable 
solution? The growing demand for land for agriculture and infrastructure, along with the use of 
trees as raw materials for manufacturing is accelerating deforestation, which is currently 
occurring at a rate equivalent to 18 football fields per minute (The Straits T imes, 2025). 
Furthermore, trees take decades to sequester carbon. Our planet urgently needs strategies t o 
reduce emissions, protect marine life, and foster sustainable food systems; large -scale seaweed 
farming offers a promising solution. 
Government subsidies act as a catalyst to enable large -scale seaweed farming. These funds cover 
the costs which go into equipment and construction in appropriate coastal areas. Moreover, 
subsidising the costs of training fishers can also create more job opportunities. These funds help 
cover the costs of building ropes and platforms in appropriately constructed coastal areas, and 
subsidi se training for fishers, thereby creating more job opportunities. By covering startup costs, 
this makes sustainable seaweed farming more accessible and scalable. 
Seaweed farming offers multiple environmental benefits. Seaweed reduces eutrophication by 
absorbing excess nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from runoff, preventing algal blooms 
(World Resources Institute, n.d.) . This limits competition with other marine plants, reduces die -
offs from, and prevents bacteria from depleting oxygen from decomposition. Hence, this helps 
protect marine life and restore biodiversity. Seaweed absorbs carbon dioxide which acts as an 
acidic oxide that forms carbonic acid when di ssolved in water, helping reduce ocean 
acidification. Coral reefs support 25% of all marine species despite covering less than 1% of the 
ocean (UNEP, 2026) ; by lowering ocean acidity, it can lessen coral bleaching , while providing 
more habitats for fish and invertebrates, supporting more resilient marine ecosystems especially 
with climate stressors nowadays. More importantly, seaweed grows as fast as 2 feet per day (The 

Nature Conservancy, n.d.) , and is highly efficient at sequestering large amounts of carbon in its 
biomass via photosynthesis. 
Beyond environmental advantages, seaweed farming also offers significant economic and food 
security benefits. Harvested seaweed can be consumed directly to feed families, while providing 
a source of income. Additionally, seaweed’s rapid growth, efficient c arbon sequestration, and 
lack of lignin (Energy Biosciences Institute, n.d.) make it an excellent renewable biofuel, 
providing a sustainable energy source. 1 acre of seaweed can produce up to 1 0,000 gallons of 
biofuel per year (Ullah et al., 2014) . These activities create job opportunities for local fishers and 
coastal communities, helping strengthen the local economy. 
Large -scale seaweed farming will offer numerous benefits, from restoring marine life, to creating 
stable jobs for coastal communities. Families will be able to enjoy sea weed as a nutritious staple 
food; industries will be able to utilise the sustainable biofuels as a renewable energy source. 
Additionally, higher water quality, more vibrant marine life, and healthier coral reefs can boost 
tourism and consequentially attract greater investments. Remarkably, increased carbon 
sequestration contributes to climate change mitigation, benefitting our society, and future 
generations as a whole. 
To achieve this, policymakers should introduce subsidies, implement zoning policies, and other 
clear regulations to enable seaweed farming to occur at scale. Scientists must optimise 
cultivation techniques and fertiliser compositions to maximise yield. Mea nwhile, these sites can 
promote eco -friendly marine experiences for tourism and educational purposes to spread 
awareness. We, as individuals play a vital role by choosing seaweed -based products to boost 
demand to make this solution financially feasible. 
The ocean’s “forests” can fight climate change, restore marine life, and support coastal 
communities , but only if we act now. Policymakers, scientists, and individuals must seize this 
moment to support and choose seaweed today. We can harness this hidden resource into a 
solution for our future generations, and the on ly planet we call home.

text:
Surviving in the Era of Artificial Intelligence 
In 2025, one of the last farmers in the Mexican state of Querétaro stood helplessly upon his once -vibrant, 
now-barren fields as his hometown became the “promised land” of artificial intelligence (AI) datacentres . 
Querétaro recently endured centuries’ worst drought due to substantial water consumption by tech giants’ 
warehouses full of computer servers, impacting crops and water supplies to nearby communities (Bearne, 
2025). 
With the tremendous surge in Generative AI’s popularity , more datacentres are being built around the globe . 
However, this popularity comes with a huge cost. There are thousands of servers running in these 
datacentres , converting massive amount of electricity to waste heat . To prevent overheating, datacentres 
use cooling systems; mainly water -based (WBC) and air -based cooling (ABC) , where the latter operates with 
air-conditioners and fans . Ironically, these systems consume billion litres of water annually and account for 
37% of total electricity consumed by datacentres (Mytton, 2021 ; Chen et al., 2025 ). 
This is evident from how Google and Microsoft, 2 dominant leaders in the AI industry, consumed 8 billion 
gallons of water in 2023 alone (Figure 1) . Most data centres , 42% of Microsoft’s and 15% of Google’s, are 
located in water -stressed areas like Virginia and Mexico (Hodgson, 2024). Consequently, citizens face a severe 
water crisis for basic needs and agriculture; raising conflicts of whether water is more important for 
fulfilling people's needs or to fuel technological industries . 
As the 4th largest datacentre market, Hong Kong (HK) is rapidly scaling its datacentre development, which 
account for more than 6% of total energy consumption sourced largely from fossil fuels (TVB , 2026 ). 
Research discovered that datacentres’ heavy dependence on fossil fuels for meeting energy demands will emit 
2.5Bn tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, an increase from 330M before the development of AI 
(Tiberi et al., 2025). Still, HK lacks a clear sus tainability plan and transparent power usage effectiveness 
(PUE) requirements for datacentres. Although this attracts more datacentres, the resulting energy demand and 
carbon emissions hinder HK from achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. 
Collectively, AI’s hidden water and carbon footprint will compete with citizens for a finite resource globally 
and lower climate quality in HK . 

 
 Figure 1: Google’s and Microsoft ’s Data centre Water Consumption 2020 -2023 
© Hodgson, C. (2024, August 18). US tech group’s water consumption soars in ‘data centre alley’. Financial Times . https://www.ft.com/content/1d468bd2 -
6712 -4cdd -ac71 -21e0ace2d048?syn -25a6b1a6=1 
 
This paper suggests a cooling model , liquid immersion cooling , that improves water and energy usage 
simultaneously to support sustainability . 
Immersion cooling involves submerging electronic hardware in a dielectric fluid , like mineral oils, that have 
better electrical neutralising properties and higher heat capacity than water (Kuncoro et al., 2019). This 
replaces water -intensive evaporative cooling in traditional cooling towers , eliminating the need for billion 
gallons of freshwater . Furthermore, r esearch observed that datacentres utilising immersion cooling systems 
achieve a 60% reduction in energy consumption compared to traditional cooling methods (Liu et al., 2025) . 
By alleviating the need for computer room air -conditioning and fans, immersion cooling can potentially 
reduce the PUE to 1.1 and save around 77.2% of CO 2 emissions compared to ABC (Figure 2; Figure 3). 
Firstly, water -stressed regions’ governments should mandate big companies like Microsoft and Google to 
retrofit all existing data centres with liquid immersion cooling system s within a targeted timeframe. This 
ensures no family in Querétaro faces power outages and future generations receive high quality water. 
Secondly, HK government should set stricter sustainability measures for datacentres, like a PUE limit of 1.3 
and requirement for datacentres to replace ABC and WBC with immersion cooling. In 2024, HK University of 
Science and Technology (HKUST) implemented HK’s one of the fewest immersion cooling technologies for 
sustainable AI research. Following the implementation, HKUST reported an 8 0% reduction in energy 
consumption for cooling and anticipated avoiding 900 tonnes of carbon emission annually, which is 45 % less 

than ABC (Siu, 2024). Hence, immersion cooling can benefit HK residents’ life quality by reducing carbon 
emissions and help the government achieve 2050 neutrality goal efficiently. 
 
 
Figure 2: Comparison of PUE and COP for various single -phase immersion cooling (SPIC) 
©Liu, S., Guo, S., Sun, H., Xu, Z., Li, X., & Wang, X. (2025). Evaluation of energy, economic, and pollution emission for sin gle-phase immersion cooling 
data center with different economizers. Applied Thermal Engineering , 260, 125049. 
 
 
Figure 3: Comparative pollutant emissions (tons) of various datacentre cooling technologies: 
SPICS -DRC, SPICS -CT, and ACS 
©Liu, S., Guo, S., Sun, H., Xu, Z., Li, X., & Wang, X. (2025). Evaluation of energy, economic, and pollution emission for sin gle-phase immersion cooling 
data center with different economizers. Applied Thermal Engineering , 260, 125049. 
 

Policy alone isn’t enough. we must take responsibility for our digital footprint. 
GPT-3 version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT drinks approximately 500ml of fresh water fo r answering every 20 
to 50 questions ( Gendron , 2023) . Hence, b efore using AI for trivial tasks or making Ghibli arts for a 
mere Instagram post, one must ask: “Is this worth a bottle of water?” 
While Microsoft and Google’s water consumption is rising, Amazon Web series does not report its 
annual water footprint at all . Thus, i nstead of opting for free AI platforms, consumers should choose 
providers that publish water and energy statistics transparently. 
Instead of waiting for others to take the initiative in healing the climate , let’s start improving our own 
consumption habits to make a greater impact immediately .

text:
From Awareness to Action: Why 
Sustainable Choices Must Be the Better 
Choice 
By: Daniel Poon (3036518912) 
 

Climate change is a problem everyone knows about , but most are unwilling to do 
anything about it . This clear gap between what people support and what people do is exhibited in 
energy consumption . Meaningful changes in energy consumption remain limited as fossil fuels 
are still the dominant source of global energy consumption (International Energy Agency [IEA], 
2023). This pattern can be seen in Hong Kong specifically transport, in which transportation 
remains a major source of carbon emissions (Environmental Protection Department [EPD], 
2023). These evidence s reveal how people’s awareness of an issue does not a lways mean 
changes in behavior. This phenomenon is referred to as the “intention –action gap,” where 
individuals act differently to their value towards the environment (Kol lmuss & Agyeman, 2002). 
This gap exists because sustainable choices conflict with everyday convenience. 
The solution for this gap is simple . Sustainable choices should not collide with 
convenience. Instead of convinc ing people to walk the extra mile or downgrade to using public 
transport when they would have been driving a car, reducing fossil fuel usage should be done in 
a way that does not require sacrificing convenience. People would still choose options that are 
better, cheaper, and more practical, even when they support environmental goals. Especially in 
cities like Hong Kong, the fast -paced lifestyle here make convenience an important consideration 
in decision making. Since forcing people into impractical behavio rs is ineffective, the focus 
should be on developing clean technologies that people will prefer over fossil fuels . The goal 
should be to make sustainable choices, not necessarily the right choice, but the better choice. 
A example of successful energy transition is in China. Rather than relying on individuals 
to sacrifice convenience, the Chinese government has taken action to support the electric vehicle 
industry through subsidies and industrial policy (State Council of the People’s Republic of 
China, 2020). Within China’s national New Energy Vehicle Industry Development Plan (2021 –

2035) , long -term targets for EV development and adoption were established to accelerate 
industry growth (State Council of the People’s Republic of China, 2020). As a result, EVs have 
become more competitive with traditional petrol vehicles in both price and performance due to 
such large -scale investment (International Energy Agency, 2024). This strategy has significantly 
changed consumer behavior. In 2024, EVs accounted for 40.9% of all vehicle sales in China 
(China Association of Automobile Manufacturers [CAAM], 2025). Moreover, in July 2024, the 
monthly retail sales of EVs in China reached 51.1% of the market, surpassing traditional petrol 
and diesel cars for the first time (Xinhua News Agency, 2024). By actively supporting emerging 
clean energy technology, China has proven how a large scale transition towards clean energy can 
happen by making the clean energy technology better than their alternative. 
The success of Chinese EVs also have led to positive spillover effects within other 
places . In Hong Kong, Chinese EV sales have increased . These imported EVs are not only 
competitive in pricing, but they also come with advanced features only seen on high end petrol 
vehicles. This makes EVs in Hong Kong more attractive , and in 2024, electric vehicles 
accounted for over 70% of newly registered private cars in Hong Kong (Transport Department, 
2024). By improving the desirability of clean technology for people , behavioral change s will 
naturally happen without requiring individuals to sacrifice their everyday convenience. 
This solution, where the focus is on making sustainable options the better option can also 
lead to positive climate results in different sectors outside of transportation . In the energy sector, 
improvements in renewable energy such as solar panels have led to the prices of clean energy 
being cheaper . As a result, clean energy is now more competitive with fossil fuels (International 
Energy Agency, 2023) . This show how innovation is the key to large scale behavioral change . 

Rather than relying on individual sacrifice, climate action should make sustainable options an 
upgrade , just like how people w ould prefer solar energy if it was cheaper than its alternative. 
To summarize, the solution for clean energy transition should be eliminating the 
difference between what people know and do by making the sustainable options the better 
option. Instead of asking people to downgrad e their current lifestyle, the sustainable option 
should be focusing on bettering their current lifestyle . I firmly believe g overnments must 
increase their s upport for growing clean technologies, so firms can innovate and scale to become 
the most desirable options for everyday consumers. As individuals, the next step is simple , which 
is to start choosing the better option when it becomes available.

text:
How the International Community Can Mitigate the Impacts of the Great Pacific 
Garbage Patch 
 
The Great Pacific Garbage Patch (GPGP) is now estimated to cover over 1.6 million 
square kilometers — an area three times the size of France — with an estimated 1.8 
trillion pieces of plastic swirling in its currents (The OceanCleanup, 2026) . 
 
Meet Lani, a fisherwoman from a small island in the Pacific. For three generations, 
her family’s livelihood came from the sea. But last month, she hauled in a net that 
held more plastic than fish. “The ocean is giving back what we threw away,” she told 
me. “But now my children ask why the water tastes like chemicals, and why the fish 
are gone.” This patch isn’t just a floating island of trash — it’s a toxin pump. As 
plastic breaks down, it leaches into the food chain, contaminating the fish that feed 
over o ne billion people. 
 
Yet no country is legally accountable for cleaning it up, and without intervention, 
plastic in our oceans will triple by 2040 (Simon R. & Winnie L., 2026) . Imagine a 
place so vast you can sail for days without seeing land, yet beneath your boat lies a 
floating landfill larger than many nations — invisible from satellites, ignored by 
borders, poisoning the very water that connects us all. We are leaving our fingerprints 
on the deepest parts of the Earth, and pretending we can’t see them. But Lani sees. 
Her c hildren see. And if we look closely enough — so do we. 

 
The scientific reality of the GPGP is staggering. The p atch contains approximately 
79,000 tonnes of plastic, with microplastics making up 94% of the estimated 1.8 
trillion pieces (Lebreton et al., 2018). Plastic acts as a vector for invasive species, 
allowing coastal organisms to colonize the open ocean ( José C. et al., 2021) . 
Meanwhile, humans ingest roughly a credit card’s worth of plastic weekly, much of it 
originating from seafood contaminated by degrading ocean debris (WWF, 2019) . 
 
The core tension, however, is not technological but legal and economic. The GPGP 
lies in international waters, placing it under no single nation’s jurisdiction. The United 
Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) obligates states to prevent 
marine pollution, but it lacks enforcement mechanisms (UN, 2026) . As a result, we 
face a "tragedy of the commons" (Kellie Wardman, 2026) : every country’s plastic 
waste contributes to the patch, yet no country is financially responsible for cleanup. 
 
Attempts to assign liability have stalled, with major plastic -producing nations arguing 
that historical polluters should pay, while emerging economies resist caps on 
production. This gridlock leaves Lani and her community in a cruel limbo —suffering 
the con sequences of a problem created by a world that cannot agree on who should 
solve it. 
 
The international community must abandon the unworkable pursuit of assigning 

blame and instead implement a two -pronged mitigation strategy. First, the UN must 
pass a binding Plastic Pollution Treaty that includes an Extended Producer 
Responsibility (EPR) clause —requiring corporations to fund cleanup based on their 
historical plasti c output (Global Plastic Action Partnership, 2026) . Second, we must 
immediately scale up proven technologies like The Ocean Cleanup’s passive systems 
while creating a global "Blue Bond" fund, financed by a small tax on virgin plastic 
production, to support fishers like Lani in transitioning to debris -harvesting 
cooperatives (European Union, 2026) . If nothing changes, what is lost is not just a 
species of fish, but an entire way of life —Pacific Island cultures, the health of one 
billion people, and the very integrity of the ocean commons. The water does not 
belong to any one flag, but it connects e very single one of us. 
 
Here is the clear, specific call to action: by next year’s UN Ocean Conference, every 
citizen must demand their government sign a treaty that makes plastic producers pay 
for what they pump into the sea —and until then, refuse single -use plastic as if Lani’s 
children were your own.

text:
Singapore Breathes, Hong Kong Suffocates: 
Mandating Green Facades to Break the Air -Conditioning Trap 
 
On a July night in Kennedy Town, Kenneth Fan sat waiting for a spot to sleep in a 
community cooling centre. His apartment was unbearable , concrete walls still radiating the day’s 
heat at midnight , but running the air conditioner all night would wreck his family’s budget. Across 
Hong Kong, millions face the same impossible choice every summer, trapped in a cycle where the 
machines meant to cool them heat the city . 
Hong Kong’s relationship with air conditioning has become a public health crisis disguised 
as a comfort. Air conditioners consume 31% of the city’s total electricity, and electricity generation 
accounts for over 60% of its greenhouse gas emissions (HKUST D ivision of Public Policy, 2022). 
This energy -intensive cooling feeds the urban heat island effect: dense concrete towers absorb 
solar radiation by day and radiate it back at night, raising urban temperatures up to 5°C above 
surrounding rural areas (South C hina Morning Post, 2023). Between 2022 and 2024, Hong Kong 
recorded up to 56 “hot nights” annually , nights where temperatures never drop below 28°C 
(Earth.Org, 2025). By 2100, projections suggest 150 such nights per year. The hotter the city gets, 
the harder its air conditioners work; the harder they work, the hotter it gets. 
Hong Kong should mandate green facades, vertical greenery systems integrated into 
building exteriors -on all new developments and major retrofits, adopting the regulatory model that 
Singapore has refined since 2005. The solution is not speculative; it is proven, scalable, and already 
transforming a comparable Asian city. 
Singapore’s Building and Construction Authority requires all new buildings to meet 
minimum energy performance standards under the Green Mark scheme, with mandatory greenery 

replacement through its Landscaping for Urban Spaces and High -rises programme (National 
Climate Change Secretariat, Singapore, 2025). The Skyrise Greenery Incentive Scheme funds up 
to 50% of installation costs for rooftop and vertical greenery, having supp orted over 300 hectares 
of urban greening since 2009. The results are tangible: peer -reviewed research demonstrates that 
green facades reduce indoor temperatures by up to 3 -4°C and cut cooling energy loads by 10 - 31% 
through shading, evapotranspiration, an d thermal insulation (Wong et al., 2020). Singapore now 
aims to green 80% of its buildings by 2030. 
Hong Kong could implement this in three steps. First, amend the Building Energy Codes 
to require vertical greenery coverage on at least 30% of exposed fa cades for all new developments 
above ten storeys . Second, establish a Skyrise Greenery Fund modelled on Singapore’s scheme, 
subsidising 50% of retrofitting costs for existing buildings, prioritising public housing estates 
where heat vulnerability is greatest. Third, integrate green facade performance me trics into the 
existing BEAM Plus green building certif ication, creating market incentives for developers to 
exceed minimum standards. The estimated cost is offset by reduced electricity bills: if green 
facades cut cooling loads by even 15% across Hong Kong’s commercial building stock, the annual 
electricity s avings would be substantial, given that air conditioning alone consumes over 49 
terajoules citywide (EMSD, 2023). 
The beneficiaries are immediate and widespread. Elderly residents in subdivided flats, most 
vulnerable to heat -related hospitalisation , which rises 4.5% per degree above 29°C (Legislative 
Council of Hong Kong, 2021) , would gain cooler indoor environments without the crushing burden 
of higher electricity bills. Building owners would see reduced operating costs. The city as a whole 
would lower its carbon footprint while reversing the concrete -canyon aesthetics that make Hong 
Kong’s streetscapes feel oppressiv e in summer. 

The cost of inaction is equally quantifiable. On current trajectories, the projected shift from 
56 to 150 hot nights annually would triple heat -related hospitalisations among the elderly, push air 
conditioning from 31% toward a majority share of electricit y demand, and lock in a feedback loop 
where only wealthier residents can afford to escape the heat they collectively generate. Every year 
of delay raises both the retrofitting bill and the public health toll. 
The next step is within reach for any reader: write to your District Council member and 
demand that green facade requirements be included in Hong Kong’s next Climate Action Plan 
review. One email, one specific ask. The infrastructure exists; the science is settled; the regulatory 
model is proven. What is missing is political will , and that begins with public pressure. 
Kenneth Fan should not have to choose between sleep and solvency. No city that calls itself 
world -class can cool its residents by heating the planet. Singapore breathes because it decided to. 
Hong Kong can too , but only if it chooses green walls over grey ones.

text:
“As the Sea Dies, We Die”: Saving Hong Kong’s Oceans Through Community -Led 
Marine Protected Areas and Sustainable Fishing 
In 2024, a fisherman in Sai Kung pulled up his nets and found more plastic bags and jellyfish 
than grouper. His grandfather once filled the same boat with fish in a single morning. Now 
some days he returns with almost nothing. The water is too warm, the re efs are bleaching 
white, and the sea that fed generations is dying. As the sea dies, we die. 
Hong Kong’s coastal waters are in a critical crisis. Local coral communities suffered large -
scale bleaching events in both 2022 and 2024 due to marine heatwaves. Coral bleaching was 
again recorded at seven sites in summer 2025 (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation 
Department, Hong Kong Reef Check 2025 ). At the same time, up to 3.2 billion microplastic 
pieces (“Hong Kong Drains Pour Billions of Pieces of Microplastics into the Sea Every 
Day.”, CUHK 2023 ) flow from the city’s storm drains into the sea ever y day, and fish stocks 
have collapsed under decades of overfishing. And the worst of all, o nly about 5 –6% of Hong 
Kong’s territorial waters are currently protected as Marine Protected Areas ( “Designated 
Marine Parks” , Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department ). Hong Kong’s fishing 
industry still supports over 10,000 local fishermen and generates hundreds of millions in 
annual value, yet decades of overfishing have pushed iconic species like the Hong Kong 
grouper toward local extinction. On a globa l scale, oceans are losing coral reefs and fish 
faster than they can recover. Coral reefs supports 25% of all marine life, have lost half their 
cover since 1950 with climate -driven heatwaves accelerating the collapse. Now, the ocean 
problem had become a s ystems -level crisis t hat is already directly impacting various sectors 
of our society, for instance our food security, coastal protection, and our city’s long -term 
resilience is all at risk. 
At first glance, t he problem may sound too overwhelming to tackle , but the solution might be 
simpler than you think. I n the context of Hong Kong, simply expand ing MPAs with 
community -supported sustainable fishing has already been proven effective in preserving fish 
population s. Currently H ong Kong has eight marine parks and one marine reserve covering 
roughly 8,517 hectares (“Designated Marine Parks” , Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation 
Department ), however, it only accounts for less than 5% of HK’s coastal region . Another 
example, s cientists in WWF -Hong Kong have identified seven priority sites including Sai 
Kung, Hoi Ha Wan, Pak Nai, and other s that urgently need stronger protection. These 
protection include establishing new no -take zones, prohibiting destructive fishing and run 
active restoration of habitats and nature systems. Coral nurseries, mangrove planting and 
ghost -net removals are all necessary and effective actions to make. Looking at successful 
accounts, WWF’s Reviving Our Corals project has already planted hundreds of coral 
fragments with 90% survival rates (“Reviving Our Corals” , WWF Hong Kong 2025 ), well-
managed no take zones see substantial fish population recovery, two - to five -fold within 
merel y 5 years (“Recommendations for Pak Nai Marine Protected Area ”, The Nature 
Conservancy 2025 ). These are already proven cases of progress . 
Moreover, HK’s traditional fishermen do not lose their living, instead they gain from 
healthier fish stock s while the city gains natural typhoon barriers from restored mangroves 
and reefs. All fishermen need to do is to receive some training, better gear, and fair prices for 
eco-friendly catch through models like the WWF Seafood Guide. Eco-protection should be 
treated as smart management that fuses sustainable ideals with conventional industries, 
systems thinking in action, conservation and people working together instead of putting 
people out of jobs. The key to success is to make everyone a shareholder , make t he positive 

or negative impact visible and tangible, aligning targeted protection and market incentives to 
create win -win outcomes. Fishermen can keep their identity and income , Hong Kong families 
receive healthier local seafood. All of humanity inherit cleaner beaches, richer biodiversity, 
and a stronger defence against climate change for the generations to come. 
Citizens can contribute meaningfully to ocean conservation by consulting the WWF -Hong 
Kong Sustainable Seafood Guide to select green -listed species and by participating in local 
restoration efforts such as mangrove planting and beach clean -ups. When scaled , these 
actions generate market pressure and public momentum for stronger government policies and 
expanded marine protected areas. Having thi s integrated approach exemplifies a system atic 
thinking and synthesises insights from food systems, economics, and urban sustainabilit y, 
demonstrating that conservation can deliver co -benefits for biodiversity and livelihoods rather 
than trade -offs. 
As the sea dies, we die. But when we choose to protect it, we give life back to Hong Kong’s 
waters , and to ourselves. The choice is ours, right now .

Tang Ka Ho 3036220371 A reﬂection on global warming as a lacto-ovo vegetarian Recalling the buzzing sound of mosquitoes and the unbearable heat, I woke up several times and had a hard time falling asleep last night. The weather is getting hotter, and global warming has forced me to switch my air conditioner on when it is only April — not even summer yet. Being a lacto-ovo vegetarian, I have always thought about how much I reduce my carbon footprint to save the Earth such as how many hours of air-conditioner is equivalent to the carbon I have saved. After enrolling in this course, I have gained a new perspective on my dietary habit and global warming (particularly after the lecture on food systems). Below is my reflection as a lacto-ovo vegetarian on global warming. "Why don't you eat meat?" Whenever I make new friends, they ask me that kind of questions. Growing up in a family that adopts a vegetarian diet and has a tradition of worship, I have been given the concepts that slaughtering is cruel and that karma applies to everything we do since I was small. Gradually, I became a lacto-ovo vegetarian as I grew up. Not wanting to explain too much to my friends, I often use animal welfare and environmental protection as my answers. However, there have been times when I felt uncertain about how I contribute to mitigating global warming through my dietary habit. Yet, this course has given me determination to maintain my dietary habit for environmental protection. Being able to contribute to mitigating global warming with every meal I eat, I should be proud of myself and confident that I have made the right dietary choice. But I did not always feel this way. Whenever I have lunch with my friends, I am probably the only person who orders a vegetarian dish or I get the same order every time, I feel like I am a bit “odd”. I have asked myself questions like how much carbon have I saved as I see almost no change in global warming, whether the carbon they produced outweighed the carbon I have saved as all my friends are eating their chicken or beef in front of me. "Cheese also contributes a lot to greenhouse gas emissions, stop deceiving yourself into thinking you are a god stopping global warming." Sometimes, my friends challenge me with words like that. Not wanting to debate, I often end the conversation with a smile and a nod. "Even though it is true, I am helping compensate for the carbon emissions from the beef you guys are eating." I have this answer in my mind, but I don't say it. I don't want to be rude and I respect my friends. 

"Let's try out the vegetarian restaurant on campus for lunch later." I felt I was understood when my friend invited me last week. I suddenly knew that I could affect my friends as well, and that I helped reduce carbon emissions of my friends. After the discussion in the food systems lecture, I realized I have many companions worldwide who are doing the same thing as me. Although most of us are not adopting a full vegetarian lifestyle, I feel understood. The effectiveness of adopting a vegetarian diet to reduce greenhouse gases was agreed upon in the lecture. To my point of view, it is impossible to restrict what people eat, but my actions are being valued. The lecture strengthened my determination to continue my dietary habit. Although my e\orts toward greenhouse gas reduction may be negligible, I feel proud that I have a much lower carbon footprint than most people around me. I should not stop doing something right just because most people are not doing it. I believe my actions will be valued, and I can even inﬂuence others to reduce their emissions. What I need from people is not for them to follow what I do or praise me for saving the planet. I just want them to stop being skeptical of me and stop thinking I am a 'troublemaker' or ‘special guy’ when I am the one trying to save the planet. In the future, I will continue my dietary habit and try to become a vegan — for personal reasons and to contribute even more to greenhouse gas reduction. From now, I am proud and conﬁdent of saying I am a vegetarian to my friends and colleagues.

text:
10 years ago , we could see Tai Mo Shan across Victoria Harbour at the Peak, now we could 
not, not because buildings blocking it, but the particulates and pollutants in the air lowering 
visibility , and the trend is continuing[1]. And we are breathing in this polluted air right now , 
harming our heart and lungs. 
Motor vehicles, especially diesel burning trucks and cars are directly contributing to street -
level pollution, we can feel it when we stand near the end of a bus. Heat from hot engines 
generate nitrogen oxides and the combustion process in engines produces carbon dioxide, 
carbon monoxide and carbon particles, which diesel engines produces higher portion of 
carbon particulates. However, this only contributes to around half of the pollution we see 
today[2]. The other half is regional smog which comes from ele ctricity generation like coal or 
natural gas power plants, although improving, still accounts for 47% of sulphur dioxide in 
Hong Kong’s air[3], a source of pollutants that cannot be missed. 
Here is a solution consisting of two parts. Part one is already in progress, which is for 
transportation to fully go electric, not only for private cars, but for heavy trucks and busses. 
Electric vehicles allow us to bring pollution away from streets, as t hey produce no air 
pollutants, are more energy efficient, and their nature of using electric power builds the 
foundation in setting zero pollutant emissions for transportation. However, 68% of the 
electricity they use are still generated by fossil fuels[4], and that means the pollution is just 
transferred not fixed. This does not mean going electric is useless, this just means we have 
more work to do. 
This brings us to second part which is to stop using fossil fuels in electricity generation. One 
might immediately think about installing solar panels and windmills, they could produce 
enough electricity for a small home, and they are renewable energy that could lower the 
reliance on fossil fuels. However, at least for now solar panels are not efficient in converting 

solar energy enough, and their dependence on conditions like weather means using them to 
power a whole city is not going to work . So here is the proposed solution, to go nuclear. Why 
it works? 1 kg of uranium generates electricity produced by 300 million kg of coal[5], and the 
power plants only produces hot water, and small amounts of manageable nuclear waste that 
decay themselves. Some might fear the danger of nuclear energy after previous accidents 
such as Chernobyl that caused many deaths. From lecture a t week 4, w e see even taking these 
accidents into account, the death caused by nuclear power plants like these disasters per TWh 
is 0.03 , which is much lower than 24.6 of coal mining and their gas pollution , even the 
seemingly harmless solar panels and windmills have 0.05 and 0.04 respectively due to 
maintained and mining rare earth minerals. Here is why nuclear energy is the proposed 
solution for air pollution in Hong Kong, it is statistically safest and can produ ce electricity 
efficiently , meeting out demands without air pollution. 
What could we do to help implementing the solutions ? We could choose electric when buying 
cars, or to choose public transport that uses electricity such as MTR, as well as voting for and 
supporting policy that support other public transport to go electric. Secondly, for successful 
implementation of using nuclear energy for our air, our understanding of this form of energy 
and the fear towards it determines how difficult it is to implement nuclear energy. We could 
educate ourselves about how nuclear energy i s a greener choice, and that speaking from 
statistics it is even safer than renewable energy and of course better than coal. We could stop 
the fear and resistance towards going nuclear. 
Starting from today, choose electric, educate ourselves and others about nuclear energy and 
sustainability , support building nuclear power plants , and with the support and help we might 
save everyone’s heart and lung, and see clear air in Hong Kong after years of pollution.

text:
For weeks, I felt paralyzed by the scale of it all. Eight million tons of plastic enter the ocean 
every year. The amount is jaw -dropping , equivalent to dumping a garbage truck into the sea 
every minute. What could any individual action possibly accomplish against that tide? 
In Week 8 of our course, as we explored how the sea , which covers over 71% of Earth’s 
surface and the prosperity of all life, regulates global climate while absorbing the b urden of 
human activity, I stood on the metaphorical shoreline of our collective future. A single 
photograph of a turtle entangled in a ghost net , shown in lecture, etched itself into my 
mind: an animal even more ancient than dinosaurs , killed by our selfishness and 
carelessness. That image crystallized the tension: the ocean gives us lif e and stability, yet 
we treat it as a sink for our waste. 
Across the semester, the evidence accumulated like drifting microplastics. We examined 
how the ocean acts as Earth’s primary thermostat, absorbing vast amounts of heat and 
carbon dioxide, yet plastic pollution is the killer of this quality . Every year, millions of tons of 
plastic enter marine ecosystems and fragment into microplastics that disrupt the food web 
from plankton to tuna to humans. Traditional Western science often frames the ocean as a 
resource to be quantified and exploited, overlooking the rel ational, local-based knowledge 
of Pacific Islanders who have lived with and protected these waters for millennia. But I’ve 
learnt to recognize that indigenous communities in low -lying atolls are not just victims of 
rising seas and plastic -choked fisheries, but holders of solutions rooted in reciprocity with 
the marine world. 
Furthermore, when we connected global ocean crises to Hong Kong’s 2100 horizon , I 
realized that the problem was closer than I expected. As a coastal city reliant on maritime 
trade and vulnerable to sea -level rise, Hong Kong mirrors the ocean’s plight: our Victoria 
Harbour and surrounding waters already show signs of plastic accumulation from dense 
urban runoff and shipping. A study from the Duke University Press in 2021 revealed how 
global supply chains flood the seas with single -use packaging. Yet, one important thing I 
learnt from this course is that we should look for direction rather than despair. We explored 
how decolonized approaches could reshape responses: community -led monitoring in the 
Pacific that combines traditional ecological knowledge with modern tools . In Hong Kong’s 
context, this could mean policies that hold corporations accountable for packaging while 
empowering local initiatives to clean and restore our own marine environments. 
It is ironic, the very system that gives us life has been turned into a waste storage. Yet within 
that same story lies resilience and the real possibility of redemption. The future is not yet 
sealed. 

Instead, clear and hopeful pathways are within our reach . For starters, w e can hold 
companies accountable through extended producer responsibility laws, requiring 
manufacturers to reduce their packaging. Furthermore, we can enhance technologies that 
intercept plastic in rivers before it reaches the sea while supporting community -led 
cleanups like giving them donations. And here in Hong Kon g, we can integrate decolonized 
science into both education and policy, training the next generation to combine rigorous 
data with traditional wisdom for ocean governance that actually works. 
These steps are concrete. Pacific nations like Germany are s upporting “blue economy” 
models that significantly cut down on single -use plastic with the aforementioned methods . 
What remains is the will to scale them through personal habit shifts like refusing single -use 
items, supporting refill infrastructure and collective advocacy of pushing for bolder climate 
policies that address ocean health as central to Hong Kong 2100. 
Critics may argue that the above remedies like deposit-return schemes and blue economy 
frameworks may fail to achieve true transformation. Reasoning that d eposit-return systems 
may encourage single -use consumption through financial incentives and Pacific blue 
economy models sometimes prioritize growth over deep indigenous stewardship . 
That being said, these limitations overlook their demonstrated power when properly 
designed. Germany’s scheme has achieved a consistent 98% return rate, slashing litter and 
enabling high -quality closed -loop recycling far beyond conventional systems. Fiji’s Blue 
Economy Framework was developed through inclusive consultations with customary 
owners, explicitly integrating traditional knowledge as a core foundation. Paired with 
production caps and community governance, these tools provide tangible, decolonized 
pathways progress towards ocean recover y. 
Finally, the semester taught me that knowledge without narrative remains shallow, and 
narrative without action is hollow. I leave with a commitment: to advocate for ocean 
solutions that are scientific and actionable. The waves are still rising , but so can our 
response.

text:
The Climate Residency Pathway: 
Hong Kong's Answer to the Rising Tide 
Ioane Teitiota is a citizen of Kiribati, a sinking Pacific Island nation with an average 
elevation of only three meters. As sea temperatures rise, water in wells becomes undrinkable 
and crops die. In 2015, he applied for refugee status in New Zealand but was deported. In 
2020, the UN ru led that deporting climate refugees could violate their right to life. 
However, looking around the world, many cases like Ioane's are happening. Eighty -four 
percent of climate refugees are from vulnerable countries. The World Bank predicted that by 
2050, climate change could force 216 million people to move within their own c ountries, 
with 49 million in East Asia and the Pacific. Those who contribute the least suffer the most. 
Yet, facing this crisis, the international community is responding slowly. The 1951 UN 
Refugee Convention does not recognize climate change as a reason for moving to another 
region permanently. 
Luckily, New Zealand has opened a new page to this scenario. In 2017, the government 
proposed to create visas for climate refugees from Pacific islands, offering 100 visas for 
Tuvaluan and Kiribatian applicants. Learning from New Zealand, Hong Kong, as a w ealthy 
region, is responsible for carbon emissions and handling climate refugees. A "Climate 
Residency Pathway" should be implemented, granting climate refugees five years of legal 
status to live in Hong Kong. This could balance humanitarian protection and local needs. 
Specifically, under this scheme, applicants must come from UN -recognized vulnerable 
countries, such as Tuvalu, Kiribati, coastal Bangladesh, and the Sahel region, to avoid fraud. 
In the first two years, the refugees can work using protected status. In the third and fourth 
year, they can apply to continue staying. In the fifth year, if they have shown they have 

worked for protecting Hong Kong's climate for 1,200 hours or more — which means 20 
hours per month — then they can apply for permanent residency. New arrivals of climate 
refugees must work for Hong Kong's climate corps, planting mangroves, maintaining floo d 
barriers, and assisting in disaster training. Therefore, refugees become active contributors but 
not passive receivers. 
However, s ome might doubt whether this scheme is feasible, but it is feasible. New Zealand 
has already shown its viability in 2017. Plus, the UN is implementing credit projects led by 
climate refugees. They are not burdens. Instead, they could provide Hong Kong with valuable 
labor. More importantly, Hong Kong itself is facing its own aging problem. By 2041, the 
labor force will be reduced by 2.1 million. Climate refugees could fill the shortage of Hong 
Kong's labor and make contributions to the city's envir onmental resilience. The World Bank 
pointed out that, after careful management and monitoring, population shifts could let people 
escape from poverty and build a stable, climate -resilient life in a new environment. 
Then, for funding, Hong Kong should impose a climate levy on high -emission industries, 
such as power generation. It emitted 32.5 million tonnes of CO2 in 2022. Even a 1% tax 
could generate substantial revenue to support this climate refugee pathway. Plus, this can 
ensure those who contributed to the problems are responsible for the consequences. They 
cannot ignore the poor or powerless. 
Therefore, under this scheme, everyone will benefit. Climate refugees gain dignity and safety 
while Hong Kong gains thousands of new workers to address our aging population. The 
World Bank predicts 216 million could lose their homes by 2050. If we act now, Hong Kong 
could be a good example for other wealthy areas to learn from. The climate crisis will be seen 
and paid attention to. Last but not least, actions can be taken by us today. Follow a local 
climate advocacy organization such as Climate Action Hong Kong on Instagram. Share their 

posts and tell your friends: "I support Hong Kong accepting climate refugees. Do you?" 
When more people speak up, the government cannot ignore us. Every share, every post, every 
conversation is significant to policy changes. Hong Kong, as a wealthy city, m ust take 
responsibility. 
In summary, the sea level is rising. Kiribati and other regions are already sinking. Hong Kong 
is responsible for taking care of climate refugees. Building a Climate Residency Pathway can 
protect climate refugees and meet Hong Kong's own needs.

Pacific islands.

leading climate refugee visas work.

text:
Fast fashion: The price we don ’t see 
 
Today’s fashion is cheaper, faster, and more convenient than ever. 
A few clicks, and a new outfit arrives at your door. But what we 
don’t see is the price paid elsewhere - in depleted rivers, 
poisoned fields, and the silent suffering of farming communities. 
For countries like Bangladesh, the rise of fast fashion has brought 
not prosperity, but a slow environmental collapse that directly 
threatens the land and the people who live from it. This essay 
addresses those hidden costs, showing the real impact of our 
disposable wardrobe on agriculture, and why the convenience we 
enjoy comes at a price most of us never pay. 
The current scale of worldwide textile production in staggering - 
with production nearly tripling from 2000 to today, now sitting at 
almost 150 billio n articles of clothing manufactured each year , 
which equates to around 12 to 16 articles of clothing for every 
person on earth. Rampant as it is - this trend shows no sign of 
stopping, with estimates suggesting textile manufacturing to only 
grow in the upcoming years. Consumers now -a-days are buying 
60% more clothing than they did 15 years ago and are keeping 
them for only half as long - leading to a culture of hyper -
disposab ility. To meet this demand, the industry has adopted a 
philosophy of ‘Dynamic Assortment ’ - which means coming up 
with new designs constantly - resulting in a significant portion of 
manufactured clothes not even being sold, instead getting 
dumped in landfills or incinerated . 
This enormous wave of manufacturing clothes comes at an 
equally enormous cost. Accounting for all the stages of 
production (raw material s to final product), garments consume a 

huge amount of water - from a simple cotton t -shirt that needs 
2,700 litres to a leather tote bag estimated to consume over 
17,000 litres of fresh water - around 8 0% of which is discharged 
back into nature as untreated wastewater carrying a toxic mixture 
of synthetic dyes, heavy metals, and other chemical s. Then there 
are the greenhouse gas emissions - fast fashion is now the 
second largest contributor to global CO 2 emmisions - accounting 
for about 10% , which is more than global aviation and maritime 
transport combined. Another less-known aspect of fast fashion ’s 
negative impact on the environment is it s emission of 
microplastics - synthetic fibers like polyester are the fourth 
largest source of primary microplastics in the oceans. Laundering 
these clothes releases roughly 500,000 tons of microfibers per 
year - the equivalent of dumping 50 billion plastic bottles into the 
sea. On top of all that, fast fashion also consumes colossal 
amounts of fossil fuels and other non -renewable resources - 98 
million tonnes of oil are estimated to be used each year to create 
synthetic fibers, and the textile industry also accounts for nearly 
20% of global insecticide use and 10% o f pesticide use. 
All these negative factors manifest as a death sen tence for the 
agriculture of nations like Bang ladesh. The waste water 
discharged as a by -product of textile manufacturing dam ages the 
rivers and canals - transforming them into toxic conduits of heavy 
metals and synthetic dyes. This industrial runoff also poisons the 
silt, chemically contaminating the soil which resu lts in long -term 
loss in cultiva tion viability. Furthermore, the industry's massive 
consumption of pesticides , fertilizers and insecticides creates a n 
"open loop" that collapses local biodiversity and exhausts the 
water table. For millions of farmers like my grandfather, this 
systemic extraction means that the very resources required for 

their food security and social mobility are being hijacked to fuel 
disposable global trends. A customer in the west buys clothes 
and accessories for cheap, and the price, in turn, is pai d by the 
farmers and their families with the ir food, livelihood and life. 
The numbers tell a simple truth: fast fashion is starving farmers in 
Bangladesh while filling closets in the West. But it’s still not too 
late. We can force brands to pay for recycling. We can incentivise 
farmers to grow clean cotton . We can ban the destruction of 
unsold clothes. These aren’t fantasies - they have precedent with 
laws already passed in Europe and Australia. What’s missing is a 
worldwide call to action . As consumers, we must demand 
durable, sustainable clothing and vote with our wallets 
accordingly . As global citizens, we must hold the fashion industry 
accountable for every litre of water stolen and every field 
poisoned. Change is possible - but only if we stop looking away .

text:
The Silent Collapse: The Impact of Warming Oceans on Fishermen 
In downtown St. John’s, fishing nets are pulled, but only 700,000 tons of wild salmon were 
caught , compared to 2.8 million tons of farmed salmon (Seafood Society, 2024). By 2048, 
seafood may vanish, leaving only jellyfish. It seems unbelievable, but this is a fact. Rising 
ocean temperatures is a major driver —over 90% of the past 50 years of warming has been 
absorbed by oceans ( Lindsey & Dahlman , 2025). The livelihood of fishermen now depends 
on sustainable marine practices. 
Unsustainable practices accelerate this crisis . First, o verfishing reduces carbon sequestration , 
while trawling disturbs accumulated carbon stores . 0.34-0.37 Gt of carbon dioxide were 
released annually —equivalent to emissions from over 66 million cars (Atwood et al., 2024). 
Moreover, marine pollutants thickened the greenhouse veil . Rising sea temperatures also 
damage habitats, reducing fish populations . Bleaching -level heat stress scarred 84% of reefs 
globally and destroyed spawning grounds , leaving less polyps and shelter for zooxanthellae —
the base of marine food . Fist population fell, endangering fishermen’s survival worldwide . 
Without imminent actions, global temperatures will surpass the Paris Agreement threshold , 
pushing marine ecosystems toward s collapse . (Hamilton and Feit, 2009, as cited in 
Chandrima Shaw et al., 2023) . 
Sustainable marine practices must be implemented both locally and globally . To begin with , 
the community, notably schools , could hold annual coastal clean -ups and recycle plastics to 
reduce greenhouse effects . Such collective action s are vital, since 79% of plastics end up in 
the environment (Geyer et al., 2017, cited in Shaw et al., 2023), releasing carbon dioxide and 
methane through photo -oxidation. More critically , the tiny microplastics pulverised from the 
estimated 640,000 tonnes of fishing gears lost in the oceans annually are made from synthetic 
plastics and accelerate the emission intensity. (Eurofish International Organisation, 2023) . 
These initiatives foster environmental responsibility from a young age, with research 
stressing that children develop responsibility through activities that connect their actions to 
others (Dementiy & Grogoleva , 2016) . 

 
(Shen et al., 2020) 
Building upon community efforts, government s could also enforce fishing bans to restore 
biological carbon pump . Increasing fish populations elevates carbon sequestrations , since fish 
store carbon and expel the rest as sinking pellets . Indeed , nearly 30% of all carbon 
sequestered by marine organisms is linked to fish (World Maritime University, 
2025) . Complementary measures in corpora te establishing a local r egistration system for 
fishing vessels, limiting new entrants , maintaining sustainable fishing levels , and designating 
fisheries protection areas (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, 2023) . In 
these areas, restocking periodically could enable growth and reproduction to restore marine 
resources (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, 2023) . Furthermore , 
indigenous knowledges offer generational guidance for ecosystem restoration , since the y 
include tracking, sustainable fishing and appropriate use of marine resources . Equally 
important , the government should prohibit trawling to reduce damage to the seabed and 
minimize carbon release. Instead, selective gears could be introduced - for instance, excluder 
leadings , which separate codends of varying mesh sizes (Feekings et al., 2023 ). 
Additionally , artificial reef (AR) project s should continue to enhance fisheries resources. 
Monitoring surveys highlighted local ARs host higher abundance and diversity of fish than 
natural habitats, notably commercially valuable breams and snapper s, which use them for 
shelter, feeding and reproduction (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, 
2023) . Various types of AR may be deployed based on material availability, deployment 
purpose and site conditions (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, 2023) . 

Most ARs, such as concrete blocks and old vessels , enhance habitat complexity . Others serve 
as biofilters to improve water quality or act as anti-trawling devices to protect nursery and 
spaw ning grounds . Taken t ogether, these measure s safeguard the livelihoods of coastal 
communities. 
Admittedly, p ro-development advocates may contend that sustainable marine practices 
reduce short -term profits for fishers. Nevertheless, by 2100, annual losses from climate 
change for just 16 major U.S. fisheries could range between $278 to 901 million (Moore et 
al., 2020) . This demonstrates that without sustainable marine actions , we cannot guarantee 
human existence, fishermen’s livelihoods, and economic stability in the long run. Therefore , 
fishermen should join the training sessions offered by local government s in transitioning 
toward sustainable marine practices , to adapt more effectively to new measures (Agriculture, 
Fisheries and Conservation Department, 2023) . These sessions usually cover knowledges 
such as the use of selective fishing gears and recreational fishing. For policymakers , 
legislation against unsustainable practices , increase d financial allocation s into artificial reef 
projects and public encourage marine protections are essential . Ultimately , every individual 
should bear the responsibility to advocate for ocean conservations , including recycling 
plastics and supporting products labelled with marine sustainability. 
The invisible , imminent impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities are often 
overlooked until we go off the boundary and are confronted with alarming numbers . The 
silent collapse is reversible, but only if we act now. Saving our oceans is not optional - it is a

text:
1 
 Clearing the Air: A Reflection on Hong Kong's Air Pollution Crisis 
Word: 702 
 
Agnes has run a newspaper stand in Central for twenty years, breathing the heavy 
exhaust generated by buses and ferries. “I’m used to it,” she told reporters in 2025 (HK2050 Is 
Now, 2025). Her statement is striking not for its persistence, but for what it reveals about 
normalization. In the same year, air pollution was responsible for 3,508 d eaths in Hong Kong 
and imposed an economic burden of HK$42 billion which is not from a disaster, but from 
breathing (Clean Air Network [CAN], 2025). 
 
Working on my collage about Hong Kong’s air crisis compelled me to confront a number I had 
previously regarded as abstract. In 2024, roadside nitrogen dioxide levels reached 65 µg/m³ 
which is 550% above the World Health Organization guideline, while fine p articulate matter 
exceeded safe limits by three times (CAN, 2025). These are not distant statistics. They are the air 
outside the classroom, the bus stop, and the wet market. Globally, air pollution accounts for 
approximately seven million deaths annually (Lau et al., 2023). What troubles me most is not the 
scale of the problem but how thoroughly Hong Kong has learned to accept it. 
 
 The solution I believe in is one that remains underemphasized in local climate discourse: 
prioritizing the replacement of diesel engines in public and commercial transport. I am proposing 
that the mandatory and accelerated electrification of the entire public transports such as buses, 
taxies, minibuses, and more should be enforced through binding legal tim elines rather than 

2 
 aspirational roadmaps. This approach is not radical, instead it represents a necessary realignment 
of policy priorities. 
 
Interestingly, current policy attention mostly favors private vehicle electrification, as 
they posses greater political visibility. But private cars sit in garages for most of the day. A diesel 
bus does not. It runs twelve to sixteen hours daily through th e decent corridors in one of the most 
densely populated cities on earth. Although road transport contributes approximately 20% of 
Hong Kong’s total greenhouse gas emissions, commercial vehicles account for the majority of 
direct and street -level pollution exposure (Environment Bureau, 2021). Individuals like Agnes 
are not affected by emissions, they are exposed to the exhaust of vehicles throughout the day. 
The effective solution has to be designed around patterns of actual exposure, not ownership. 
 
 The proof that this work s is thirty minutes away by MTR, Shenzhen. They achieved a 
significant reduction in average air pollution levels by fully electrifying their public transport in 
2019 (HK2050 Is Now, 2025). Hong Kong already established a policy framework, including the 
2021 Electric Vehicle Roadmap and subsequent updates in 2024 and 2026 (Environment and 
Ecology Bureau [EEB], 2021, 2026). But in late 2024, only 0.86% of buses and 0.17% of 
minibuses were gas -free (Business Environment Council, 2025). Three binding steps would turn 
it into an achievable plan. First, by implementing electric -only procurement for franchised buses 
like Citybus by 2027. Second, by establishing legall y binding electrification targets for 
minibuses by 2030. Lastly, by introducing transition subsidies funded through diesel tax 
revenues to support operators facing financial constraints. 
 

3 
 Research indicates that residents in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas face 
significantly higher mortality risks from air pollution than those in wealthier populations (Wong 
et al., 2008). Outdoor workers, elderly residents residing near major roads, and children in older 
school buildings are exposed to the risks in high chance. These are the people who cannot opt out 
of environmental risk. Thus, cleaning th e shared air is the only intervention that reaches all of 
them at once. Importantly, there is a clear avenue for civic engagement. The Legislative Council 
is currently reviewing the Air pollution Control Bill 2024, while the government has proposed 
maintai ning nitrogen dioxide targets (CAN, 2025). This Bill Committee is accepting public 
submissions now. Even a single letter is highly encouraged to paint the sky blue. 
 
Agnes is used to the air. That sentence should be unbearable. A city that has made peace 
with 3,508 preventable deaths a year has stopped being ambitious on behalf of its people. Hong 
Kong has the evidence, the policy architecture, and a neighbor that has already proved the 
alternative is possible. Now, it is time to make changes.

text:
Should Hong Kong mandate a sustainable seafood labelling scheme to reduce overfishing caused by overconsumption? In the 1980s, Sai Kung sea-urchin diver Ng Wai-keung could fill buckets in one morning and earn thousands of dollars daily. By the late 1990s, the same reef produced almost nothing. Overfishing had stripped away the algae his urchins depended on, forcing him to quit fishing and ending a four-generation livelihood (China Daily, 2017). His story raises an urgent question for Hong Kong: should the city mandate sustainable seafood labels to reduce overfishing driven by overconsumption? Hong Kong’s seafood appetite is unusually high. Using FAO data, a government-commissioned study estimated seafood consumption at 77.5 kilograms per person per year, placing Hong Kong second in Asia and sixth globally (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department [AFCD], 2011). WWF-Hong Kong later estimated that in 2017 each resident still consumed 66.5 kilograms of seafood, more than three times the world average (WWF-Hong Kong, 2017). Local waters unfortunately cannot keep up with the surging demand. Assessments of 17 common marine fish species found 12 to be heavily over-exploited and the other five fully exploited, while the biomass of bottom-dwelling fish has fallen by roughly 90 percent since the 1970s (Lee et al., 2025). This suggests that overfishing in the city is mainly caused by overconsumption. Globally, overfishing is a serious problem that 

requires urgent action, as it depletes key species, weakens ecosystem balance, and damages marine food webs (NOAA, 2024). For that reason, I propose Hong Kong should mandate a sustainable seafood labelling scheme, since the current market conceals ecological costs from consumers. Most diners cannot know whether a fish comes from a depleted fishery or a less destructive capturing method. As such, overfishing remains invisible when people make choices and purchases. A mandatory scheme would enable this unrevealed information visible. The government can build on WWF-Hong Kong’s existing traffic-light Seafood Guide, and require major supermarkets, chain restaurants, and seafood retailers to display labels consisting of four details on every seafood item: “species name”, “origin”, “fishing method”, and a “coloured rating” (green for “better choice”, yellow for “use less”, and red for “avoid”). Such labels are easy to understand, while the detailed explanation can be accessed through WWF-HK or government websites. I believe this approach is far more effective than simply awareness campaigns, as it serves to fill a real information gap. Despite voluntary guides already existing, they depend on consumers searching for them voluntarily in advance, unlike the mandatory labels which reach consumers at the exact moment of purchase. Research on seafood ecolabels found that clear and credible labels can shift market share toward certified products and can sometimes support modest price premiums (Roheim et al., 2011). In 

Hong Kong, where seafood is often bought rapidly in wet markets or ordered without much thought in restaurants, that matters a lot. Although the labels cannot solve overfishing on their own, they can change the demand pattern significantly, which directly targets Hong Kong’s major cause for overfishing. A possible criticism to the proposed labeling scheme may be the disproportionate burden on local small businesses. This concern is reasonable, and hence the policy should be phased in. Large supermarket chains and franchised restaurant groups can comply first, owing to their centralised procurement systems and greater capacity to absorb administrative costs. Smaller wet-market stalls could follow afterwards at later phases with governmental support. The proposed labelling scheme’s benefits go far beyond stickers on menus. For consumers, it provides clear and immediate information that makes sustainable choices easier at the moment of purchase. For retailers and importers, it creates pressure to move away from red-rated species and source more responsibly, especially when reputation and consumer trust are at stake. Over time, this could largely reduce demand for the most vulnerable fish, ease pressure on depleted stocks, and support the recovery of stressed fisheries. It may also encourage a broader cultural shift in Hong Kong, making seafood sustainability part of ordinary consumption rather than a niche environmental concern. 

Readers need not wait for legislation. They can open WWF-Hong Kong’s Seafood Guide today, screenshot the red list on their phones, and avoid those species at their next hotpot, sushi restaurant, or family seafood dinner. If more and more consumers do this, formal labelling will become much easier to justify. The Hong Kong government should legislate a mandatory sustainable seafood labelling scheme now. Without clear labels, overfishing stays hidden behind everyday consumption. A science-based law would not solve the crisis overnight, but it can at least expose the truth. Once the menu tells the truth, choosing differently becomes possible. Word Count: 747 (excluding title and references)

Desert in the depths: Hong Kong’ s vanishing urchins. China Daily Hong Kong Edition. Lee, T., Chan, K., & Wong, P. (2025). Status of Hong Kong demersal fish stocks after the trawl ban. International Journal of Culture and History, 11(1), 29–31. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. (2024). How does overfishing threaten coral reefs? Roheim, C. A., Asche, F., & Santos, J. text:
Community Composting as a Climate Solution 
Did you know that the meat chops and greens that you have not consumed 
completely for yesterday’s lunch and mix it with other waste in a trash bag which was 
transport to the landfills would emit methane in the air, causing serious global 
warming effect when the cumulative effect of more people and more time is taken 
into calculation. 
The food waste problem is becoming severe and alarming among Hong Kong 
and globe. Food waste which cannot decompose completely in landfills would 
produces methane that contributes to global warming (Wong & Yang, 2023). A large 
amount of greenhouse gases would be released from the process of food 
decomposition. 10 percent of Hong Kong's carbon emissions are coming from 
landfills used for waste disposal (Landfills set for closure by 2035 amid green push, 
2024) and food waste accounted for 29 per cent among three major classifications of 
munici pal solid waste in 2024 (Environmental Protection Department, The 
Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, 2025) . This 
relationship shows the influence of food waste made in the landfills on the greenhouse 
gases emissions. The situation in the global level looks the same. Food loss and waste 
represent 8-10% of annual global greenhouse gas emissions which leads to 
considerable biodiversity loss (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate 
Change, 2024 ). These facts prove that we must develop a feasible solution to cope 
with this challenging puzzle. 
Based on the situation, an effective method is to promote a system for using 
kitchen waste composting in processing point , which could not only reduce the 
amount of food waste that is transported to landfills, but also provide benefits to the 
community garden by composting the kitchen waste into fertilizer . Inhabitants could 

complete garbage classification at the source and use the accumulated manure to 
fertilize the crops in the garden . The specific steps include establishing standardized 
compost bins in each community. The kitchen garbage could be put into these 
processing points for closed fermentation . After the biochemical reaction, the garbage 
could be transferred into useful fertilizer. Compared to the traditional landfills, this 
method makes good use of waste materials and gets benefits from it. Waste food will 
no longe r emit methane and carbon dioxide into the atmosphere limitlessly but act as 
the one step of the recycling process. This measure also implies weakened urban heat 
island effect as the building of gardens which increases the number of greenbelts in 
the city. This solution could be implemented in three steps: Firstly, establish 
processing points in each community and educate professional staff . Secondly, 
encourage residents to do garbage classification to divide the kitchen garbage by 
giving away some gift s like daily necessities. Finally, in the long term, the processing 
point could be equipped with in each unit such as office buildings and schools. These 
steps could make sure the project has a nice implementation. 
The system could not only decrease the greenhouse gas emissions observably, 
weaken the global warming issue , but also provide fertilizer to each resident. For the 
actions that could be finished immediately at the individual level , we could first try to 
do garbage classification at home after meals . This is to say, set two trash cans which 
are divided into kitchen garbage and other waste. Next, we could vote for the 
policymakers to enact relevant legislation to guarantee the implementation of the 
solution as on the beginning point, some citizens may tend to keep unchanged. Hence, 
the legislation is a strong and forceful measure to ensure implementation. 
In conclusion , this system could decrease the amount of garbage in the landfills 
that do harm to the climate and provide fertilizer to the participants, reaching a win -

win landscape for both the environment and human beings.
