text:
CCGL9065 : Final Reflective Essay on 
Building a Climate Change Solution 
Name: Chum Chi Yeung (UID: 3036393427) 
 

Report 
This report ’s main focus is on the topic “Fashion and climate change” . Despite fast fashion’s 
effects on the global climate has been studied frequently, not much people are aware of how 
pollution occur s at both ends of unwanted clothings’ lifecycles. I hope to show you perspectives 
on the effect of fast fashion on climate change, use real -life stories to display an 
underconcerned climate problem, and bring up relevant and practical solutions , and connect 
them into a combined narrative. 
According to various sources, fast fashion is a growing industry with a ever -growing market 
size – the fashion industry reached $2.4 trillion by 2019, and employs over 75 million 
(Villemain , 2019 ) – a lot of people’s livelihood depend on it. About industrial impacts, we 
should know that its annual water consumption is 93 billion cubic meters – 4.6 million times 
the annual average of showering ( HKWSD, 2011). Moreov er, it accounts for around 2 to 10 
percent of global emission – more than that of av iation and shipping industry combined 
(Villemain, 2019 ). You may think that travelling by ships or aeroplanes emit more pollutants 
than producing the shirt you wear on ; now is a chance to think again – hope the data convinces 
you otherwise. 
The pollutions caused by fashion industry is sort of overdocumented – the story below is about 
how clothes pollute even when they are donated. 
Africa is considered as a “landfill site” for unwanted textiles. However, in 2020, a documentary 
filmed in Africa (European Environmental Bureau, 2020) , ended up subvert ing expectations . 
You may assume that donating unwanted textiles to poor nations can provide suffecient 
clothing to the needy , but the reality is the opposite: African interviewees stated that the 
enormous amount of imports “killed” the local textile industry, and the unwanted textiles were 
dumped in landfills which polluted local rivers and caused floods . This further cause more 
water -based adverse health effects . Elsewhere, storms cause the massive clothing landfill in 
Ghana to flood sewers, and more worse, pollute the ocean (Besser, 2021). 
Crossing the Atlantic, a similar situation occurs in the Atacama Desert, Chile . Ever since the 
country open ed up its borders decades ago, tonnes of clothes have flood ed the local market. 
After sorting, unwanted clothes are dumped in the open desert, and (occasionally) set on fire. 
Toxic smoke are released which causes multitudes of respiratory diseases for locals ( Barlett, 
2024). 

You think you are less guilty when you put your unwanted wears in a bin because you thought 
you are “helping the needy” . This end up polluting their water sources , forcing them to breath 
in polluting gases, and cause them to loose their homes due to flooding. Is it surprised that your 
act causes more problems to them? If you acknowledge the problem, would you try to seek 
better alternatives to fast fashion ? 
It is kinda pointless to argue about who is responsible for the damages caused by fashion 
industries – everyone is equally responsible , as shown by the example below. You purchase d a 
new shirt online because a pop star wears it, the company accumulate d orders and commision ed 
a factory in South Asia to manufacture them, then the factory leaders decide d to have the 
wastewater dumped in the nearby river, and when a local man drink ed from it, he became ill 
due to toxification. Solutions are sought by going to the top of the problem itself instead of 
fixating on accusations , yet, “consumer responsibilities” remain a s the first-step in fixing the 
overall issue. 
With rising awareness, “slow fashion” is presented as a foremost alternative , defined as a 
“different approach in which designers, buyers, retailers, and consumers are more aware of the 
impacts of products on workers, communities, and ecosystems” (Vito, 2022). Consumers like 
us should try thinking differently in adapting “slow fashion” . Obviously, the most practical 
method is to shop less – as less demand causes less supply , and less impacts . Despite second -
hand clothing may be seen as unappealing, this has changed with time – especially as pop stars 
like A. Hathaway and O. Rodrigo (Igoe, 2025) have been advocat ors of it. Choosing second -
hand clothing is a further step in preventing textiles going to waste . It benefits both your wallet 
and the environement . 
A different side of fashion industry’s damages on the global climate is shown. The pollution 
caused by textile disposal are as impactful as that cause d by manufacturing. As customers, we 
bear significant responsibility o n fashion pollution , and the problem can only be solved through 
increased awareness and collective work on reducing demands and supplies.

text:
In a Hong Kong supermarket, a shopper picks up a neatly packaged beef imported from Brazil. What she cannot see is that, in São Paulo state, farmers suffering from drought desperately watch their rivers shrink. Where does their water go? Ask the cattle. Every kilogram of beef consumed in Hong Kong carries an invisible 15455 litres of water, enough to fill a small swimming pool, mostly for growing feed crops. while the average Hong Kong resident’s food-related water footprint stands at 4727 litres per person per day, almost double the Mainland Chinese average, due to high consumption of animal products (Hong Kong Water Supplies Department, 2024; Vanham et al., 2019).

Hong Kong imports 95% of its food, meaning the city's food consumption is almost entirely embedded in goods produced elsewhere, yet none of this hidden water cost appears on the label (EEHB, 2011). Globally, agriculture accounts for over 70% of freshwater withdrawals worldwide (FAO, 2020). Hong Kong's diet-driven demand quietly amplifies this pressure while remaining entirely invisible at the point of sale.

This invisibility is not inevitable—it is a choice. Hong Kong should introduce a phased, mandatory water footprint label on imported food products. This is a standardized panel disclosing litres of water consumed per 100 grams, similar in design to existing nutritional information, combined with a public education campaign and incentives for lower-water proteins. The methodology already exists. The Water Footprint Network provides internationally recognized accounting standards applicable across food categories (Hoekstra et al., 2011). 

The behavioral aspect is strong. Building on Thaler and Sunstein's nudge framework, research consistently finds that visible, standardized labels shift purchasing choice without restricting them. One controlled study found nutritional labels produced a statistically significant 7% reduction in high-calorie purchases (Freedman & Brochado, 2010). Critically, simplicity matters that color-tiered labels in the front of the pack outperform complex numerical data in changing purchase intention (Graça et al., 2019). A green-to-red tier alongside a single number would allow shoppers to grasp relative water intensity in seconds. This makes the recognition process simple, shifting consumer preference for a large number of water intensive food products, creating real market pressure on the most water-intensive imports, and will then result in reduced water usage in production.

The rollout need not be abrupt. A realistic Hong Kong model would begin with a voluntary pilot in Year 1, engaging major supermarket chains to trial water footprint disclosure on red meat, dairy, and rice. Mandatory coverage of all imported food and packaged goods would follow in Year 3, enforced through the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, which already administers Hong Kong's nutrition labelling regulations. This phased logic mirrors Australia's Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme, which had already saved over 300 megalitres of water daily and delivering household bill savings of one billion Australian dollars per year (Waterwise, 2021).

If successful, this initiative would significantly lower Hong Kong’s overall virtual water footprint, ease pressure on global water-stressed regions, and set a model for other import-dependent cities. Hong Kong families, students, and future generations would benefit from greater awareness and healthier eating patterns. Restaurants and canteens could innovate with attractive low-water dishes, potentially creating new market opportunities.

However, Critics will argue that a sharp drop in beef demand could harm beef producers’ livelihoods. Many farmers and workers in the supply chain depend on stable export markets; sudden shifts risk unemployment and economic instability in rural communities. To mitigate this, transition measures such as financial support, technical assistance for sustainable farming, and gradual implementation are essential. Agricultural subsidies should redirect away from high-water industrial beef production toward diversified, so together with the labelling policy, agroecological farming can work simultaneously on both demand and supply side.

WWF-Hong Kong has already called for labelling systems empowering consumers to make sustainable food choices (WWF-Hong Kong, 2023). You can add your voice by writing to the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department on food safety labelling. Or, you can simply track your own meals for three days and calculate the virtual water used (try the HK Water Footprint Calculator). Then, replace one beef dish with a lower-impact option. Small consistent choices, multiplied across 7.5 million residents, create real impact. The label is not a ban—it is a mirror. 

To recapitulate, Hong Kong’s appetite for beef hides a massive water debt that affects the world. By making it visible and supporting a fair transition for producers, we can enjoy food responsibly while protecting shared resources. The choice is on our plates.

Word Count: 744

text:
In 2020, a family in Bangladesh, was forced to leave their livelihoods as farmers, and rent a small 
place in Khulna. One of the farmers’ names is Hossain. “I’m leaving my father’s address forever,” 
he says. “All my relatives including my four brothers have lived here for several decades. Frequent 
natural disasters prevented us from living in our own homes. The other brothers left long ago. I 
was the last one. ” (Guardian News and Media , 2020). 
Natural disasters have become increasingly frequent in the past decade, and the power of it has 
been going up. In Hong Kong, the 5 worst typhoons in Hong Kong history happened within the 
span of 9 years. Let’s just take Super Typhoon Ragasa 2025 as an exam ple. 22 flooding cases were 
reported across Hong Kong, including in the unfortunately typhoon -susceptible Heng Fa Chuen 
and the Fullerton Ocean Park Hotel, which went viral for a clip that showed tidal waves crashing 
through its glass doors and flooding th e entire hotel lobby. (Time Out Hong Kong, 2025). We were 
lucky that these typhoons did not cause catastrophic events like in Bangladesh. Hong Kong also 
has plenty of low -lying areas, do we really want it to become like Bangladesh one day and we will 
be forced to move to away from our homes? 
If we look at natural disasters from a bigger picture, it is caused by increasing global temperature , 
and it seems that c oncern is growing that temperature rises above 1.5°C are beginning to be seen 
as inevitable, or even acceptable, to powerful members of the global community. Rises above 
1.5°C increase the chance of reaching tipping points in natural systems that could lock the world 
into an acutely unstable state. (Atwoli et. al, 2021) My solution to this involves cooperation 
between the government, the public, and people from the vehicle sector. Specifically for Hong 
Kong, since a lot of carbon emissions come from vehicle emissions (20% of carbon emissions in 
Hong Kong), the government should penalize the public more for buying traditional vehicles and 
provide more subsidies to electric vehicles. In parallel to that, the government could start providing 

electric vehicle charging spaces to all carparks in Hong Kong, so that it is more accessible and 
more convenient to use electric vehicles. This is a major step to reducing carbon emissions by 
reducing the proportion of traditional vehicles on Hong Kong roads. Using China as an example, 
an electric vehicle technological innovation research was carried out. For many years, exploration 
and practice of the scientists has proved that the electric vehicle system can be improved 
significantly . Key areas were targe ted to reduce GHG emission by the strengthening of institutional, 
legal, economic, and technological instruments and hence to achieve energy conservation, energy 
structure optimization as well as ecological improvement. (Liu, R., Li, M. H., & Zhang, H. N. 
2017) . If you walk in the streets of China nowadays, you see electric vehicles everywhere on the 
road, proving that this solution is feasible. Not only in China, electric vehicles have also become 
a trend and more people are buying it on a global basis. Hong Ko ng is behind in development of 
electric vehicles compared to the globe. To implement this solution, the government should get 
sufficient consultation from the public, then cooperate with electric vehicle companies to provide 
more electric vehicles, and imp rove the accessibility to electric vehicle charging facilities in the 
city. By improving electric vehicles’ supply and its accessibility, the public would be more 
incentivized to buy these types of vehicles along with respective taxes and subsidies mention ed 
earlier. 
The benefits of this solution are simple and long -term. The government gets to make one step to 
combat climate change by reducing carbon emissions and catch up with the globe in technological 
development. The public would be able to contribute to mitigating global temperature increasing 
by using electric vehicles instead of traditional ones and reducing their overall expenditure on 
transport as fuel is not needed for electric vehicles. What are you waiting for? Go ahead and buy 
an electric vehicle now and c ontribute to mitigating climate change! 

To sum it all up, do you want Hong Kong to suffer the same fate as Bangladesh in 50 years? If 
not, then go ahead and buy an electric vehicle to replace your traditional vehicle, contribute to 
reducing carbon emissions. Every small step of every one of you contributes to one big step to 
deal with climate change and make these natural disasters less disastrous to our daily lives!

text:
The Hidden Water Debt: A Call for HK Fashion Revolution

A shopper in Causeway Bay often picks up a new cotton T-shirt without much thought. However, this purchase involves more than spending HK$199. Producing one T-shirt requires about 2,700 liters of water, which equals what one person drinks over 900 days (World Bank, 2019). This concept is known as “water debt.” This unseen cost reveals the hidden impact of everyday consumption.

This hidden cost reflects a broader global issue. Fast fashion places pressure on water resources worldwide, and Hong Kong is part of this system through its consumption. The city discards large amounts of clothing each day. According to Redress, Hong Kong throws away about 402 tonnes of textiles daily, which equals around 17,480 suitcases (Redress, 2025). Each item contains “virtual water” used during production. As a result, Hong Kong consumes global water resources and then wastes them.

This pattern becomes more serious in a local context. Hong Kong depends heavily on external water sources, importing 70–80% of its fresh water from the Dongjiang River (Water Supplies Department, 2026). Climate change is making this supply less stable. Therefore, this issue is not only environmental but also a matter of local security.

Given these challenges, Hong Kong needs a clear and practical response. The government should adopt a two-part strategy, regarding both consumption and waste. Together, we aim to reduce the city’s overall water footprint.

The first step focuses on transparency. The Legislative Council should introduce a mandatory “Water Disclosure Ordinance” (Information Services Department, 2024).

Under this framework, retailers would be required to display a standardized “Water Consumption Grade” on every product tag, similar to the energy efficiency labels currently found on household appliances. This system is essential because many consumers currently lack the data necessary to evaluate the environmental cost of their wardrobes, leading to uninformed purchasing decisions that favor high-impact fabrics. Clear labeling would encourage consumers to choose low-impact materials. Examples include recycled polyester and linen, which use less water than virgin cotton. Ultimately, providing clear, regulated information serves as a critical tool for guiding the public toward more sustainable consumption habits.

The second step focuses on building a circular system. While labeling helps consumers make informed choices, it does not address the large volume of existing textile waste. Therefore, the government should establish the “Kwai Chung Circularity Hub” in underused industrial areas. By leveraging the Industrial Building Revitalisation Scheme to provide rent subsidies and infrastructure support, the government can attract specialized green-tech businesses to the area. A core component of this hub would be the deployment of “Fibre-to-Fibre” (F2F) recycling technology (Hong Kong Research Institute of Textiles and Apparel, n.d.). This advanced process is capable of separating complex blended fabrics, like cotton-polyester, into high-quality reusable raw materials. To ensure the commercial viability of this hub, the government should offer tax incentives and "Green Credits" to fashion brands that adopt this technology for their supply chains. Such an approach transforms textile waste from a management burden into a valuable economic resource, effectively reducing the city's landfills usage.

These reforms would empower citizens. Consumers currently face limited information when making purchases. This situation often leads to “blind consumption.” Water labeling would give people more control over their choices. It would allow them to act according to their values. At the same time, the recycling hub would lower the cost of sustainable materials. This change would make ethical fashion more affordable. Sustainable clothing would no longer be limited to a small group of consumers. More residents could participate, which would strengthen a sense of shared responsibility.

These changes would also improve regional security. Hong Kong depends heavily on the Dongjiang water supply. Reducing the city’s water footprint would lower this dependence. It would also reduce the risk of shortages and price changes. This approach supports the “Total Water Management Strategy.” It would also ease pressure on waste systems. Therefore, circularity is not only an environmental goal. It is also a practical strategy for long-term stability.

The era of invisible consumption must end. Every clothing purchase carries a hidden water cost. The next time you reach for a new garment, ask yourself if the fabric is worth the water debt it carries. We must demand legislative transparency and support local circularity today, or risk a tomorrow where our taps run dry.

Final Portfolio Essay 
Yim Tsz Chun Angelo 
UID: 3036515726 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

In September 2023, residents of Wong Tai Sin in Hong Kong were left speechless after a 
proclaimed “once -in-500-years” storm transformed not only their MTR station, but also their 
main roads and malls into rivers. However, as time passed, these extreme weat her phenomena 
only became increasingly frequent. 
 
As a coastal city, Hong Kong is seeing typhoon warning signals appear with increasing 
frequency, all thanks to climate change. Increasing temperatures and sea levels from melting 
ice across the globe allow more storms to develop, while also spreading more warm air flow 
towards different parts of the world. Icelanders are now facing mosquitoes, a species of insect 
that has not been able to inhabit Iceland until now, thanks to record -breaking heat from warm 
airflows. The temperature in Iceland last year recor ded a 1.1°C increase from the averages 
from 1991 to 2020, the highest it has ever been. 
 
To combat climate change, one first requires an understanding of climate change. According 
to a study done by Which? and London Economics on UK retailers (Team, 2025), 88% of 
products with green descriptions in the market provided no justification or conte xt, along 
with nearly 65% having unclear and vague green claims. These claims not only give 
misinformation to consumers, but also utilise the desire for sustainable shopping among the 
public to gain more profits. Governments should enforce regulations on a dvertising 
campaigns, including climate -change -related elements, to banish greenwashing, companies 
portraying a false image of environmental friendliness, in marketing and avoid climate 
change misinformation. 
 

Upon understanding the urgency of climate change, possibly destroying our home, are you 
going to take action immediately, or wait it out and watch as the Earth plummets into chaos? 
Priority to deal with climate change should be emphasised by everyone to sa ve our home. 
Governments should reallocate funds and plans towards climate -proofing impact -prone areas, 
as well as research and development of technologies to help alleviate climate change. 
Flooding -prone areas can be researched, utilising natural features , such as trees, to reduce the 
impact of flooding. Cities facing constant high temperatures can also be climate -proofed 
using natural features by changing the urban landscape and natural features. Research and 
development can also be oriented on geoenginee ring projects, to help combat the phenomena 
of climate change, and protect the livelihoods of the public, with ongoing examples of 
Aerogel and Carbon Dioxide Removal Methods. 
 
Everyone needs to take part, not just the government. Industries, particularly food and 
fashion, should reshape to minimise waste. Clothing manufacturers should focus on 
environmentally friendly qualit ies and lower output to control the amount of waste from 
clothes each year. Restaurants should charge extra for food waste, and recycle them into 
fertilisers for farming. Most importantly, each individual should revise their daily routines 
into more sustainable habits. Avoid throwing wearable clothes away; rec ycle them into mops 
or donate them to those in need. Leftovers can be kept and eaten the next day. Stand up to any 
injustice by protesting and reporting the trouble -makers, whether its firms exceeding their 
quotas for pollution when producing, or governments for ignoring and neglecting climate 
change rules or targets. Only by acting as one can we effectively combat climate change. 
Combating climate change would make everyone’s livelihoods better. As the general public, 
cities would not constantly face extreme and disruptive weather, which would not happen as 

often, and pollution, guaranteeing safety. The Global Environment Outlook, Seventh Edition 
(GEO -7), report on December 9, 2025 (Environment, 2025), predicts that such climate -
change combating measures would avert 9 million premature deaths by 20250. From t he 
perspective of the government, the economy would boost , with fewer disruptions from 
extreme weather. A more comfortable city allows higher productivity in infrastructure 
building, and attracts more tourists to visit. The GEO -7 predicts that under lowere d climate 
risk, macroeconomic benefits will surge starting in 2050 until 2070 by reaching USD 20 
trillion per year. From the perspective of the ecological cycle, the extinction of animals due to 
a changing climate would be alleviated . Forests, coral reefs, and wetlands will allow the 
coexistence of different animals, allowing survival for many species. 
 
If alleviating climate change helps all of us, why don’t we pursue it? Is it only when climate 
change becomes too severe that we will then understand the need to change our actions? 
Earth gave our civilisation resources to expand and develop; it’s our resp onsibility to keep 
Earth healthy. If residents of Hong Kong from the year 2100, who are constantly facing 
typhoons and heat strokes, are now looking at your actions, what would you do?

Heat Inequality in Hong Kong: Who Gets to Stay Cool? Hua Yanjing U3036573302 At 2 a.m. in Sham Shui Po, an old cleaner tries to sleep in a subdivided room. His fan is turning, but the air still feels like hot soup. Outside, Hong Kong looks bright and rich. Behind glass walls, luxury flats and malls keep air-conditioners running. Buildings use about 90% of HK’s electricity, and this power creates over 50% of the city’s carbon emissions (GovHK, n.d.). In 2024, Hong Kong had 50 Hot Nights, so this night is not rare now (Hong Kong Observatory [HKO], 2025a). The cleaner wants to switch on the air-con, but he thinks about the bill first. Hong Kong is heating up, but the heat is not equal. HKO shows that the annual mean temperature rose by 0.14°C per decade from 1885 to 2025. The speed became faster from 1996 to 2025, reaching 0.35°C per decade. In 2024, Hong Kong recorded its warmest year, with 24.8°C annual mean temperature and 52 hot nights. Under a very high emissions pathway, Hong Kong may face 152 extreme hot weather every year by 2081 to 2100 (Hong Kong Observatory, 2025, 2026). These numbers show that heat is already inside daily life. For rich people, heat just means a higher bill. But for those poor families, heat can mean bad sleep or even losing dignity. My solution is a “Cool Home, Cool Street” programme. The idea is simple. Hong Kong should treat cooling as basic protection, but not a luxury. The programme should start in Sham Shui Po, Kwun Tong, and old new-town areas. Dense buildings, old flats, and many low-income people are gathered in those places. The programme requires a public heat-risk map. The map should combine HKO temperature data, urban heat island data, and census data on subdivided units. In 2021, Hong Kong had about 108,200 subdivided units, and 215,700 people lived in them. Their median floor area was only 11.0 square metres (Census and Statistics Department, 2023). This data can accurately tell the government where help should go first. It should not only follow rich districts or property value. The project also needs a “cooling repair kit” for poor homes. The kit can include reflective window film, better exhaust fans, and government subsidy for efficient air-conditioners. The subsidy should go to tenants. Landlords should promise that they will not increase rent after improvement. NGOs can check whether the action has been actually implemented. The street also needs cooling. Many people leave hot rooms and go outside, but the street is also burning. The city should add shade at bus stops, wet markets, playgrounds, and public housing entrances. Trees are useful, but trees are farly not enough. Hong Kong also needs covered walkways, drinking water points, and cooling rooms opened at night during Hot Night warnings. 

 This plan works because it makes the housing and the community better with the support of data. Research in Hong Kong found that during extreme heat, areas with strong urban heat island effects had almost twice the mortality risk compared with more moderate areas. Elderly people aged 75 or above were especially vulnerable (Ho et al., 2023). In HK, heatstroke leads to more than 200 hospital admissions each year, with about 2 to 5 deaths annually, mostly between May and September (Centre for Health Protection, 2025). Heat is not just uncomfortable; it can become a serious health danger. The people who benefit most are subdivided-flat families, elderly residents, outdoor workers, cleaners, security guards, or students. A cooler home can help people sleep better, work better, and study more comfortably. In addition, businesses also benefit due to the fewer sick leaves. The climate could be improved, if subsidies support only energy-efficient appliances and better building design. This also fits Hong Kong’s Climate Action Plan 2050, which promotes energy saving and green buildings (GovHK, n.d.). People can take action today. You can download the HKO app and check Hot Night warnings. You can call an elderly neighbor during very hot nights. You can set your air conditioner to 25.5°C when possible. Students can record their room temperature for one week and share the results with classmates, NGOs, or district councilors. The question we should keep asking is simple: “Who cannot afford to cool down?” Hong Kong often calls itself an efficient city. But in the age of climate change, efficiency is not enough. A good city should not only move quickly; it should also allow people to breathe. If heat is unequal, then cooling must become a matter of justice. References Census and Statistics Department. text:
The Bridge to Zero – Protecting Hong Kong's Self-Employed Drivers in the Age of Oil Crisis 
International oil prices have surged over 55% since the outbreak of US-Iran war.1 The blockade 
of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted oil supply, particularly diesel, as one-fifth of the world's oil flows 
through this strategic waterway.2 Hong Kong has no oil reserves. Local petrol and diesel prices spiked 
to a record $32 per litre3 within weeks. For self-employed minibus drivers and truck drivers, this was 
not a mere news headline. It was an immediate survival crisis. Some minibus drivers now skip lunch 
to afford the fuel.4 
Context 
Hong Kong's transport sector is the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions, 
accounting for nearly 20% of the city's total.5 The government has committed to carbon neutrality by 
2050. Yet oil and coal account for 86% of transport fuel,6 revealing Hong Kong's dependence on 
imported oil with no reserves.7 The current oil crisis makes a permanent exit from fossil fuels necessary. 
 
1 Graham, E., & Shan, L. Y. (2026, April 21). A timeline of how the Iran war shook oil prices — and 
what comes next . CNBC. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/21/oil-price-iran-war-middle-east.html 
2 Oil prices trim gains after UAE exits OPEC, OPEC+ by Reuters. (n.d.). 
https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-rise-as-no-end-to-iran-war-standoff-
seems-in-sight-4590293 
3 The Standard (2026, March 10). ‘World’s priciest oil’: Record oil prices fuel HK EV rush amid 
long burden. The Standard . https://www.thestandard.com.hk/news/article/326321/Worlds-priciest-
oil-Record-oil-prices-fuel-HK-EV-rush-amid-long-burden ; and actual data is peer reviewed 
4 TVB News (2026, March 10). HK minibus sector may increase fares in response to rising oil 
prices. TVB News. https://news.tvb.com/tc/pearlnews/69b012ee2dd2502b5884800a/TVB%20News-
HK-minibus-sector-may-increase-fares-in-response-to-rising-oil-prices 
5 RTHK 31 Green Future - Zero Emission. (n.d.). 
https://www.rthk.hk/tv/dtt31/programme/greenfuture_eng/episode/1018430 
6 Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government. (2025). Hong Kong Energy End-use Data 
2025, p.70. https://www.emsd.gov.hk/filemanager/en/content_762/HKEEUD2025.pdf 
7 LCQ5: Energy supply in Hong Kong . (n.d.). 
https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202603/25/P2026032500478.htm 

Electric alternatives cost over one million dollars – far beyond what self-employed drivers can 
afford. The government's three-month fuel subsidy provides instant relief,8 but extending it indefinitely 
would lock Hong Kong into fossil fuel dependency. Withdrawing it too soon would bankrupt thousands 
of drivers. The city is caught between an immediate survival crisis and a long-term climate imperative. 
Solution: “Bridge to Zero” Program 
This is not an either-or situation. I propose a two-phase "Bridge to Zero" program that protects 
self-employed drivers while accelerating the electric transition. 
Phase one focuses on immediate relief. The government has already implemented a three-
month fuel subsidy9 , which has significantly eased pressure — a Tuen Mun resident bus operator 
recently withdrew its fare increase application.10 I contend this is a good move and should be extended 
to 6 months, or until diesel prices return to pre-war levels, to keep the fuel affordable for struggling 
commercial drivers. However, this is not permanent fossil fuel support. It is a time-limited bridge to 
combat the price surge. 
Phase two focuses on conversion to electric vehicles to eradicate fossil fuel dependency. The 
key to accelerating the electric commercial vehicle adoption is accessibility. Given the government has 
fully waived the first registration tax on new electric commercial vehicles,11 I propose launching a 
"one-for-one replacement scheme" on commercial vehicles that provides additional concessions when 
drivers scrap old fossil fuel vehicles for new electric ones. This scheme has proven highly successful 
 
8 Consumer prices 'accelerated somewhat' in March - RTHK . (n.d.). 
https://news.rthk.hk/rthk/en/component/k2/1852191-20260423.htm 
9 Ibid. 
10 The Standard. (2026b, April 9). Govt fuel subsidies prompt Tuen Mun resident bus operator to 
withdraw fare hike application. The Standard . 
https://www.thestandard.com.hk/news/article/328939/Govt-fuel-subsidies-prompt-Tuen-Mun-
resident-bus-operator-to-withdraw-fare-hike-application 
11 Promotion of electric vehicles | Environmental Protection Department . (n.d.). 
https://www.epd.gov.hk/epd/english/environmentinhk/air/promotion_ev/promotion_ev.html#Measure 

for private cars, quadrupling electric private car ownership to over 140,000 vehicles.12 It is now time 
to launch it for commercial vehicles like trucks and minibuses. 
Critics may argue that any fuel subsidy delays the energy transition. I accept this as valid – 
indefinite fuel subsidy does hinder energy transition. However, a transition that bankrupts self-
employed drivers is politically unsustainable and morally indefensible, violating United Nations 
Sustainable Development Goals 1,8, and 10.13 Fuel subsidy is necessary to protect drivers' livelihoods 
during the transition. We cannot sacrifice the vulnerable in energy transition. 
Others may critique that electric commercial vehicles are not ready for Hong Kong’s hilly 
terrain and limited range. I understand that electric commercial vehicles face greater challenges on 
Hong Kong's slopes than private cars. However, electric vehicle technology is already sufficient. The 
expected range of a fully loaded electric truck is as high as 400km,14 which is more than enough for 
Hong Kong, let alone minibuses. The energy transition is already technically feasible. 
Impact and Next Step 
This solution benefits multiple stakeholders. Self-employed drivers gain immediate relief and 
a realistic path to electric ownership. This proposed solution would alleviate the burden on commercial 
drivers, as over 80% have reported mental and physical health impacts from high oil prices.15 The 
climate and general public also benefit, as commercial vehicle electrification reduces roadside NO2 
 
12 'One-for-One Replacement' scrapped for private EVs - RTHK . (n.d.). 
https://news.rthk.hk/rthk/en/component/k2/1844997-20260225.htm 
13 THE 17 GOALS | Sustainable Development . (n.d.). https://sdgs.un.org/goals 
14 Shoman, W., Yeh, S., Sprei, F., Plötz, P., & Speth, D. (2023). Battery electric long-haul trucks in 
Europe: Public charging, energy, and power requirements. Transportation Research Part D: 
Transport and Environment , 121, 103825. 
15 HK drivers feel pain as fuel prices soar amid global oil shock . (n.d.). Chinadailyhk. 
https://www.chinadailyhk.com/hk/article/632366 

emissions, which disproportionately affect dense neighbourhoods like Mong Kok and Kwun Tong, 
giving us cleaner air to breathe, especially in crowded areas. 
The next step is immediate and achievable. Simply write an email to the Transport and 
Logistics Bureau, “Extend fuel subsidies for self-employed drivers. Launch one-for-one replacement 
scheme for commercial vehicles. Protect the vulnerable in the energy transition.” 
Conclusion 
Hong Kong did not cause the US-Iran war. Self-employed drivers did not cause climate change. 
But both are paying the price. A just transition should not ask the most vulnerable to sacrifice first. The 
government has already shown leadership with the diesel subsidy16. Now, it must complete the bridge: 
extend the fuel subsidy and fund the conversion, forging Hong Kong towards a cleaner future.

 “Deadly Ring Tightening Humanity’s Future” : 
Increase of Space De bris continuous ly nibbl ing the road to the Universe 
Rockets and spaceships sound like one of the co olest things for most of us in 
our childhood , which symbolize the top point of human technology, and the desire for 
explor ation. However , when we shif t our gaze from the se small boats carrying 
huma nity’s hopes as they pierce through the clouds , back to the geosta tiona ry orbit . 
Tons of debris are for ming a shocking but a lso dangerous “steel star belt” around o ur 
planet. 
The amount of large r debris with size larger than 10 cm reach up to 29 ,000 
pieces, and smaller ones with size larger than 1cm and 1mm reache s 670,000 and 
190,000,000 respectively .1 According to the ES A Space Environment Report 2025, 
there were a bout 11 to 1 2 accidental fragmentat ions per year , and the 1 1 brea k-up 
events in 202 4 generated over 26 00 new p ieces of trackable debris .2 This number 
will be come even larger in future , since the amount of fragments increase, the 
possibility of collision also increase, then creating even more after collision, 
spreading the cloud of death further. This cloud may even become a large obstacle in 
humanity’s future development in space: satellites between Low -Earth Orbit and 
Geostationary Or bit is facing a n extremely high probab ility of being shot down by 
space debris , which may have a widespread influence , including defense sector, 
airline industry, marine indust ry, railway industry, roadways, GNSS timi ng, 
agricultur e. 
Solving this systems -level crisis requires moving beyond voluntary guidelines 
toward mandatory orbital "traffic laws" and active extraction. The first step is the 
enforcement of the "Five -Year Rule." In late 2024, the FCC shifted from a 25 -year 
recommendat ion to a strict five -year deadline for satellite disposal after mission

next generation of debris. However, regulation only stops the bleeding; it doesn't 
remove the 2,600 new fragments generated just last year. 
The second, more critical step is Active Debris Removal (ADR). We must 
treat the orbit like a national park that requires maintenance. Missions 
like ClearSpace -1 and Astroscale’s ELSA -M have moved from theory to deployment 
in 2025 -20264, using robotic arms and magnetic docking to capture high -risk objects. 
By targeting the "statistical triggers" —the large, defunct boosters that act as collision 
bombs —we can prevent the Kessler Syndrome before it becomes self -sustaining. 
Furthermore, shif ting to a "Circular Space Economy" where companies are 
incentivized to refuel and repair satellites rather than abandoning them turns orbital 
space from a graveyard into a sustainable industrial zone. 
The payoff of this smart management is the survival of our digital 
infrastructure. Protecting the LEO and Geostationary ecosystems secures a global 
space economy projected to hit $1.8 trillion by 20355. If we fail, the "cloud of death" 
will eventually blind our weather satellites and collapse the GNSS timing that 
synchronizes our global power grids and financial markets. We aren't just saving a 
view; we are defending the nervous system of modern civiliz ation. 
Individuals can accelerate this shift by demanding transparency from the 
private sector. Support the Zero Debris Charter by favoring telecommunication 
providers that commit to debris -neutral launches. Public pressure creates the market 
incentive for companies to invest in expensive cleanup technology. When the cost of 
polluting space exceeds the cost of cleaning it, the indu stry will pivot. 
As the orbit dies, our connectivity and safety die with it. But by choosing to 
clean our skies, we ensure that the top point of human technology remains a gateway

text:
CCGL9065: Climate-safe Housing , for the poorest 
 
(Creative common) 
Cheung Hoi Shun Marco, 3036396089 

It's hot at midnight in the room. The roof of the rooftop unit in Sham Shui Po is like a 
stove. The air is circulated by a fan. The child isn't reading a climate report. She's 
envisioning the future of Hong Kong. 
 
Globally, extreme heat is increasing in frequency and intensity, particularly in urban 
areas; the IPCC reports there is a rise in heatwaves, and heat can be magnified in cities, 
particularly during nighttime. Hong Kong is particularly susceptible due to it s high-rise 
dwellings, concrete roads and narrow roads, making it very susceptible to the urban 
heat island effect, along with aircon exhaust. But not everyone feels the heat. Hong 
Kong has 110,000 subdi vided units; 220,000 people live in small rooms that are often 
poorly ventilated and with little money to cool their homes. Hong Kong will not just test 
its climate adaptation with seawalls by 2100. It will be with the poor's capacity to live in 
their apar tments. A Climate -Safe Housing Standard is needed in Hong Kong because 
the poor should not suffer extreme heat because they are poor, live in small areas or the 
owner didn't put in a window. 
 
The standard should be taken up by the Basic Housing Unit (BHU) system. BHUs 
currently have minimal standards for subdivided units to be habitable and legally 
rented, such as size, height, fire safety, water, light and ventilation. That's a start. But 
"basic" should not be "minimal". It should not be legal to build units with a roof and a 
toilet. It should be possible to sleep and breathe in the heat. 
 
The Climate -Safe Housing Standard should ensure that all BHUs pass two tests: a heat 
test and an airflow test. The heat test would demonstrate that it is substantially cooler 
than the outside peak heat warning temperature. We could make the BHU at least 2° C 
cooler than the outside peak temperature during the day and cooler than outside 
temperature on hot nights as a trial standard in Hong Kong. This is not much, but it is 
significant. It does not promise luxury. It promises no less than the street. 
 
The air flow test would require that all rooms containing a living room or bedroom have 
at least one external window. An internal, ground floor or corridor facing window should 
not be sufficient. Have mechanical ventilation, certified to provide at least five air 
changes per hour, in the unit if this is not possible. The test should be on the property 
owner's form and be inspected. WHO guidelines on housing associate indoor 
temperature with health impact, and recommends that ventilation, shading, insulation, 
orientation and cooling can help to lessen heat stress. 
 

This will help single elderly, kids in subdivided flats, those who work outside and need a 
cool place at home, and the poor who can't afford to run aircons. Everyone would 
benefit too, with less peak electricity demand, improved sleep and the end of the 
ambulance run s. Now it's time for action. Hong Kong should mandate an application for 
a BHU be accompanied by a Climate -Safe Housing Checklist, which will measure 
indoor temperatures, must include external windows, be shown to have fresh air, 
shading, insulation and wiring for safe appliances. App roval should only be granted if 
the unit is suitable, with landlords to make necessary changes. After approval, home 
residents should be able to report hot and stuffy BHUs. If the government is to use an 
approval for a BHU status as a stamp of quality for subdivided flats, heat -safety is a key. 
 
In 2100 Hong Kong may have cut seawalls. But climate adaptation means a more 
delicate question: Will kids get to sleep on hot summer nights? Climate -proofing begins 
with climate -proofing homes.
